chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text: Life processes are the maintenance functions carried out by living organisms even when they are not doing any particular activity. These processes are essential to prevent damage and break-down, and to maintain the organised, ordered nature of living structures.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Living organisms can be identified by visible movement (breathing, growth), but molecular movement is the true criterion.
Viruses do not show molecular movement and are therefore considered borderline cases of life.
Life requires energy from outside the body (food/nutrition) to carry out maintenance.
Key life processes: Nutrition, Respiration, Transportation, Excretion.
In multicellular organisms, diffusion is insufficient to meet all needs; specialised tissues and organ systems are required.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Life processes are the set of maintenance functions that all living organisms must continuously carry out to prevent the break-down of their ordered, molecular structures and to sustain life.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Maintenance is needed because ordered living structures tend to break down due to environmental effects.
Energy is required for maintenance; this energy comes from outside the body through food.
Carbon-based molecules serve as food sources since life on earth is carbon-based.
Since food and oxygen are taken in at specific locations in multicellular organisms, a transportation system is necessary to carry them to all cells.
Waste by-products of chemical reactions must be removed by excretion.
Outside sources of energy are not under direct control of the organism and must be broken down or built up to produce a uniform energy source: oxidising-reducing reactions are common.
The process of acquiring oxygen from outside the body and using it to break down food for cellular needs is called RESPIRATION.

sections.label: EXERCISE 5.1 (In-text Questions - p.39):
sections.raw:
Q: Why is diffusion insufficient to meet the oxygen requirements of multicellular organisms like humans?
A: In multicellular organisms, all cells are not in direct contact with the surrounding environment. Simple diffusion can only supply oxygen to cells immediately adjacent to the surface. Cells deep inside the body cannot receive adequate oxygen by diffusion alone; a specialised transportation system is needed.

Q: What criteria do we use to decide whether something is alive?
A: The primary criterion is molecular movement. Living organisms show molecular movements even when there is no visible movement. Visible movement (breathing, growth) is a secondary indicator.

Q: What are outside raw materials used for by an organism?
A: Outside raw materials (food, water, minerals, oxygen) are used for: energy production (nutrition + respiration), building and repairing body structures, and carrying out chemical reactions needed for maintenance.

Q: What processes would you consider essential for maintaining life?
A: Nutrition, Respiration, Transportation, and Excretion are the four essential life processes.

items.question: What are life processes?
items.answer: Life processes are the maintenance functions carried out by living organisms continuously to prevent structural break-down and to sustain life. Examples include nutrition, respiration, transportation, and excretion.

items.question: Why are molecular movements considered the true criterion for life?
items.answer: Visible movement is not always present in living organisms (e.g., a sleeping dog, a non-growing plant). However, molecular movements inside cells are always present in living organisms and stop only at death. Viruses lack such molecular movement and are therefore considered borderline cases of life.

items.question: Why do living organisms need a continuous supply of energy? Where does this energy come from?
items.answer:
Living organisms need continuous energy because:
(i) The ordered, organised structure of living beings naturally tends to break down due to environmental effects.
(ii) Maintaining and repairing this structure requires constant work, which requires energy.
(iii) All cellular activities (molecular movements, growth, repair) consume energy.
The energy comes from outside the body in the form of food. Food is processed through chemical reactions (oxidation) to release energy for cellular use.

items.question: Why is diffusion alone not sufficient to meet the needs of multicellular organisms? What systems have evolved to address this?
items.answer:
In multicellular organisms:
(i) All cells are not in direct contact with the external environment.
(ii) Simple diffusion can only move molecules over very small distances efficiently.
(iii) Cells deep inside the body cannot receive oxygen, food, or remove waste through diffusion alone.
To address this, multicellular organisms have evolved:
- Specialised organs for intake of food and oxygen (alimentary canal, lungs).
- A transportation system (circulatory system in animals; xylem and phloem in plants) to distribute materials to all cells.
- Specialised excretory organs to remove waste products.

items.question: What happens to the energy released during cellular respiration? Why is ATP important?
items.answer:
Energy released during cellular respiration is immediately used to synthesise a molecule called ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate).
- ATP acts as the universal energy currency of the cell.
- It is formed by the reaction: ADP + Phosphate + Energy --> ATP
- When energy is needed for any cellular activity, ATP is broken down: ATP --> ADP + Phosphate + Energy (30.5 kJ/mol released).
- ATP provides energy for muscle contraction, protein synthesis, conduction of nervous impulses, and many other cellular activities.
- This is similar to a battery that can provide energy for many different kinds of uses.

items.question: Describe the relationship between the four essential life processes - nutrition, respiration, transportation, and excretion.
items.answer:
The four life processes are deeply interconnected:
(i) NUTRITION: Organisms take in food (carbon-based materials) from outside the body. This provides the raw material and energy source needed for all other processes.
(ii) RESPIRATION: The food taken in during nutrition is broken down using oxygen in chemical reactions to release energy. In aerobic respiration: Glucose + Oxygen --> Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy (ATP). This energy powers all cellular activities.
(iii) TRANSPORTATION: Since food is taken in at one place and oxygen at another, and since all cells need both, a transportation system is essential. In humans, the circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels) transports food, oxygen, and waste products. In plants, xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports food.
(iv) EXCRETION: Respiration and other metabolic reactions produce waste by-products (CO2, urea, uric acid) that are harmful if allowed to accumulate. Excretion removes these wastes - CO2 via lungs, nitrogenous wastes via kidneys in humans.
Without any one of these processes, the organism cannot survive. Together, they form the complete system of life maintenance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What are the processes which together perform the maintenance function in living organisms called?
items.explanation: The maintenance functions carried out by living organisms are collectively called life processes. Growth and reproduction are not maintenance functions. Molecular processes is too vague a term.

items.question: In which part of the cell does the breakdown of glucose (glycolysis) take place?
items.explanation: Glycolysis, the first step of glucose breakdown, occurs in the cytoplasm. Further breakdown of pyruvate happens in mitochondria. Nucleus is for genetic material; chloroplasts are for photosynthesis.

items.question: Why are viruses considered borderline cases of life?

options.A: They are very small in size
options.B: They do not show molecular movement until they infect a cell
options.D: They do not have a cell wall

items.explanation: Viruses lack molecular movement on their own and only show it after infecting a host cell. This is why they are considered borderline life forms. Size, cell wall absence, or reproduction ability are not the defining criterion here.

items.question: Which molecule serves as the immediate energy currency of the cell?
items.explanation: ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) is the immediate energy currency used by cells. Glucose is the food molecule that is broken down to produce ATP. Starch is a stored form. ADP is produced when ATP releases energy.

items.question: In a multicellular organism, if the transportation system fails, which life process is MOST directly and immediately affected?

options.C: Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to individual cells

items.explanation: Transportation's primary role is delivering oxygen and nutrients from the sites of uptake to individual cells. Without this, cells deep inside the body starve of oxygen and nutrients even if digestion and gas exchange are functioning. Solid waste excretion (defaecation) is largely independent of the circulatory system.

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: 5.2.3 How do Organisms obtain their Nutrition?

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Nutrition is the process by which an organism takes in energy and materials from outside its body and uses them for growth, development, and maintenance of life. Food is the source of both energy and materials.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: All organisms need energy and materials; however, the way food is obtained differs between organisms.
Two main types: AUTOTROPHIC (self-feeding, using inorganic sources) and HETEROTROPHIC (feeding on organic material prepared by others).
Autotrophs include green plants and some bacteria; they use photosynthesis.
Heterotrophs include animals, fungi, and most bacteria.
Heterotrophs depend directly or indirectly on autotrophs for their food.

sections.label: EXERCISE 5.2 (In-text Questions - p.45):
sections.raw:
Q: What are the differences between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition?
A: AUTOTROPHIC: Organism synthesises its own food from inorganic raw materials (CO2, water, minerals) using an energy source (sunlight). Produces complex organic molecules. Example: green plants.
HETEROTROPHIC: Organism cannot synthesise its own food; it depends on complex organic molecules prepared by other organisms. Example: animals, fungi.

Q: Where do plants get each of the raw materials required for photosynthesis?
A: CO2: from air through stomata. Water: from soil through roots. Sunlight: from the sun. Chlorophyll: present in chloroplasts of leaf cells.

Q: What is the role of the acid in our stomach?
A: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach (i) creates an acidic medium which activates the enzyme pepsin; (ii) kills harmful bacteria present in food; (iii) helps in the breakdown of food particles.

Q: What is the function of digestive enzymes?
A: Digestive enzymes are biological catalysts (enzymes) that break down complex food molecules into simpler, absorbable molecules: carbohydrates into glucose, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

Q: How is the small intestine designed to absorb digested food?
A: The inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called VILLI which greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Villi are richly supplied with blood vessels which carry absorbed nutrients to all parts of the body.

items.question: What is nutrition? Name the two main types.
items.answer: Nutrition is the process by which organisms take in and utilise food for energy and body maintenance. The two main types are: (1) Autotrophic nutrition - organism makes its own food from inorganic sources. (2) Heterotrophic nutrition - organism depends on organic food prepared by other organisms.

items.question: What is the function of bile juice in digestion?
items.answer: Bile juice is secreted by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It performs two main functions: (i) It makes the food coming from the acidic stomach alkaline so that pancreatic enzymes can act on it. (ii) It emulsifies fats - breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.

items.question: Describe the role of the pancreas in digestion.
items.answer:
The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice into the small intestine. Pancreatic juice contains three important enzymes:
(i) TRYPSIN: digests proteins into amino acids.
(ii) LIPASE: breaks down emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
(iii) Amylase: breaks down carbohydrates into simpler sugars.
The pancreas also secretes bicarbonate to make the food from the stomach alkaline, creating the right pH for its own enzymes to work.

items.question: Describe the process of photosynthesis. What are the raw materials, and what are the products?
items.answer:
PHOTOSYNTHESIS is the process by which autotrophic organisms (green plants) prepare food using inorganic raw materials and sunlight.
RAW MATERIALS: Carbon dioxide (from air via stomata), Water (from soil via roots), Chlorophyll (pigment in chloroplasts), Sunlight (energy source).
EQUATION: 6CO2 + 12H2O --Chlorophyll/Sunlight--> C6H12O6 (Glucose) + 6O2 + 6H2O
EVENTS DURING PHOTOSYNTHESIS:
(i) Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll.
(ii) Conversion of light energy to chemical energy; splitting of water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen.
(iii) Reduction of carbon dioxide using hydrogen to produce carbohydrates (glucose).
PRODUCTS: Glucose (used for energy and building the plant body) and Oxygen (released into air). Glucose not immediately used is stored as STARCH.

items.question: Trace the journey of food from the mouth to absorption in the small intestine.
items.answer:
(i) MOUTH (Buccal cavity): Teeth break food into small particles; salivary glands secrete saliva containing salivary amylase which begins starch digestion. Tongue mixes food with saliva.
(ii) OESOPHAGUS: Food moves by peristaltic movements to the stomach.
(iii) STOMACH: Gastric glands secrete HCl (creates acidic medium), pepsin (digests proteins), and mucus (protects stomach lining). Muscular walls churn food.
(iv) SMALL INTESTINE: Receives bile (from liver, emulsifies fats) and pancreatic juice (digests proteins, fats, carbohydrates). Intestinal glands secrete intestinal juice with enzymes that complete digestion. Final products: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol.
(v) ABSORPTION: Villi (finger-like projections) in the small intestine wall absorb digested food into blood vessels and transport to body cells.

items.question: Compare autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition with examples. Explain the different modes of heterotrophic nutrition.
items.answer:
AUTOTROPHIC NUTRITION:
- Organism uses inorganic sources (CO2, water, minerals) and an energy source (sunlight) to prepare its own food.
- Examples: green plants (photosynthesis), some bacteria (chemosynthesis).
- Products: complex organic molecules (carbohydrates, proteins, fats).

HETEROTROPHIC NUTRITION:
- Organism depends on complex organic food prepared by other organisms.
- Examples: animals, fungi, most bacteria.
- Types:
(i) SAPROTROPHIC: Organisms break down dead organic material outside their body and then absorb it. Examples: fungi (bread mould, yeast), mushrooms.
(ii) PARASITIC: Organisms derive nutrition from a living host, often harming it. Examples: cuscuta (amar-bel), ticks, lice, leeches, tapeworms.
(iii) HOLOZOIC: Organisms ingest whole food material and break it down inside their body. Examples: Amoeba, human beings, most animals.
(iv) MIXOTROPHIC: Some organisms can use both autotrophic and heterotrophic modes. Example: Euglena (photosynthesis in light, absorbs food in dark).
All heterotrophs ultimately depend on autotrophs - directly (herbivores eating plants) or indirectly (carnivores eating herbivores).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The green dots seen in leaf cells under a microscope are organelles called:
items.explanation: The green dots in leaf cells are chloroplasts which contain chlorophyll, the pigment essential for photosynthesis. Mitochondria are for respiration. Ribosomes are for protein synthesis. Vacuoles store cell sap.

items.question: Heterotrophic organisms that derive nutrition from dead and decaying organic matter are called:
items.explanation: Saprotrophs obtain nutrition by breaking down dead organic matter externally and then absorbing it (e.g., fungi). Parasites live on a living host. Autotrophs make their own food. Holozoic feeders ingest whole food.

items.question: Which enzyme in saliva begins the digestion of starch?
items.explanation: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) in saliva begins starch digestion in the mouth. Pepsin digests protein in the stomach. Trypsin digests protein in the small intestine. Lipase breaks down fats.

items.question: The equation for photosynthesis is: 6CO2 + 12H2O --> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O The 12H2O on the left (reactant) represents water. What is the role of this water?

options.A: It is used to dilute the CO2
options.B: Its hydrogen is used to reduce CO2 to form glucose; its oxygen is released as O2
options.D: It transports glucose out of chloroplasts

items.explanation: Water molecules are split (photolysis) using light energy; the hydrogen from water is used to reduce CO2 to carbohydrates, and the oxygen from water is released as O2. Water does not absorb sunlight - chlorophyll does.

items.question: Where does complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats take place?
items.explanation: The small intestine is the site of complete digestion, receiving bile (from liver), pancreatic juice (from pancreas), and producing intestinal juice itself. The stomach only digests proteins partially. The large intestine mainly absorbs water. Mouth only begins starch digestion.

items.question: What is the function of villi in the small intestine?

options.C: To increase the surface area for absorption of digested food

items.explanation: Villi are finger-like projections on the inner lining of the small intestine that greatly increase surface area for efficient absorption of digested nutrients into the bloodstream. They do not secrete enzymes or bile, and peristalsis is done by muscular walls.

items.question: In Activity 5.1, a leaf from a plant kept in the dark then exposed to sunlight was tested with iodine. The green areas turned blue-black while non-green areas did not. This proves that:

options.A: Sunlight alone is sufficient for photosynthesis
options.C: Water is the raw material for photosynthesis

items.explanation: Blue-black colour indicates starch, a product of photosynthesis. Since only green (chlorophyll-containing) areas turned blue-black, it proves chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis. Sunlight was available to both areas, so it cannot alone explain the difference. Activity 5.2 (with KOH) demonstrates the role of CO2.

items.question: A patient's small intestine is surgically shortened due to disease. Which of the following is the MOST likely nutritional consequence?

options.A: Inability to digest food in the stomach
options.B: Reduced absorption of nutrients due to decreased surface area

items.explanation: The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption, and villi provide the large surface area for this. Shortening the intestine reduces this surface area directly, leading to malabsorption. Stomach digestion, bile production, and protein breakdown are not directly affected by intestinal length.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Autotrophic nutrition is the mode of nutrition in which an organism synthesises its own food from simple inorganic substances (carbon dioxide and water) using an external energy source, typically sunlight. The process is called PHOTOSYNTHESIS.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The word AUTOTROPHIC means "self-feeding" (auto = self; trophe = nourishment).
Autotrophs include: green plants, algae, cyanobacteria (use sunlight); some bacteria use chemical energy (chemosynthesis).
PHOTOSYNTHESIS equation: 6CO2 + 12H2O --Chlorophyll/Sunlight--> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O
Chlorophyll is the pigment that absorbs light energy; located in CHLOROPLASTS.
Raw materials: CO2 (via stomata), water (via roots), minerals (via roots from soil).

Three events in photosynthesis: (i) Absorption of light by chlorophyll. (ii) Splitting of water molecules (photolysis) releasing hydrogen and oxygen. (iii) Reduction of CO2 using hydrogen to form carbohydrates.
STOMATA: Tiny pores on leaf surface, surrounded by GUARD CELLS. Guard cells swell when water flows in (opening pore) and shrink when water flows out (closing pore).
Excess glucose is stored as STARCH in plants.
Nitrogen (for protein synthesis) is absorbed from soil as inorganic nitrates/nitrites, or as organic compounds prepared by bacteria from atmospheric nitrogen.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.1 (p.40):
sections.aim: To demonstrate that chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis.
sections.materials: Potted plant with variegated leaves (e.g., money plant or crotons), dark room, sunlight, boiling water, alcohol, iodine solution.
procedure: - Keep plant in dark room for 3 days (to deplete all starch).
- Expose to sunlight for 6 hours.
- Pluck a leaf; trace the green areas on paper.
- Dip leaf in boiling water (to kill cells), then immerse in alcohol over water-bath (to remove chlorophyll).
- Dip leaf in iodine solution; take out and rinse.
- Observe colour; compare with tracing.
sections.observation: Green areas turn blue-black (iodine test positive for starch). Non-green areas remain unchanged.
sections.conclusion: Only areas with chlorophyll perform photosynthesis and produce starch, proving chlorophyll is essential for photosynthesis.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.2 (p.41):
sections.aim: To demonstrate that CO2 is necessary for photosynthesis.
sections.materials: Two potted plants (same size), dark room, potassium hydroxide solution (KOH - CO2 absorber), bell jars, vaseline, glass plates, sunlight.
procedure: - Keep plants in dark for 3 days.
- Set up: Plant A - with KOH (absorbs CO2); Plant B - without KOH. Cover both with bell jars sealed with vaseline for 2 hours in sunlight.
- Test leaves of both plants for starch using iodine.
sections.observation: Plant A (no CO2 available) - no starch detected. Plant B (CO2 available) - starch present.

items.question: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
items.answer: Chlorophyll is the green pigment present in chloroplasts of plant cells. Its role is to absorb light energy from sunlight and convert it into chemical energy. This chemical energy is used to split water molecules and reduce CO2 to form carbohydrates (glucose). Without chlorophyll, photosynthesis cannot occur.

items.question: How do stomata regulate gas exchange in plants?
items.answer:
Stomata are tiny pores present on the surface of leaves (and stems). Each stoma is surrounded by two GUARD CELLS.
- When water flows into guard cells, they become turgid (swollen) and OPEN the stomatal pore, allowing CO2 in and O2 and water vapour out.
- When guard cells lose water, they become flaccid (shrink) and CLOSE the pore.
- This opening/closing mechanism regulates both gas exchange (for photosynthesis) and water loss (transpiration). Plants close stomata in water-scarce conditions to prevent excess water loss.

items.question: Describe the three events that occur during photosynthesis. Where does each event take place?
items.answer:
Three events occur during photosynthesis, all within the CHLOROPLAST:
(i) ABSORPTION OF LIGHT ENERGY: Chlorophyll pigment in chloroplasts absorbs light energy from sunlight. (Occurs in the membrane system - grana of chloroplast.)
(ii) SPLITTING OF WATER (PHOTOLYSIS): Light energy is used to split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen is released as a by-product (the O2 we breathe). The hydrogen is retained for the next step. (Occurs in grana.)
(iii) REDUCTION OF CO2: Hydrogen (from water) is used to reduce carbon dioxide to form carbohydrates (glucose). Chemical energy (ATP) produced in step (i) drives this reaction. This step does not directly require light. (Occurs in stroma of chloroplast.)
Note: Some steps (like CO2 fixation by desert plants) can be separated in time from light absorption.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: In the photosynthesis equation, from which molecule is the oxygen gas (O2) released?
items.explanation: The O2 released during photosynthesis comes from the splitting (photolysis) of water molecules using light energy. This was confirmed by isotope labelling experiments. CO2 is reduced to glucose, not split to release O2.

items.question: What is the role of guard cells in a leaf?

options.B: To regulate the opening and closing of stomata
options.D: To transport glucose to the stem

items.explanation: Guard cells surround each stomatal pore and control its opening and closing by changing their turgidity. When turgid (water-filled), they open the pore; when flaccid, they close it. They are not involved in water absorption, starch storage, or glucose transport.

items.question: In Activity 5.1, the plant was kept in the dark for 3 days before the experiment. Why?

options.A: To allow maximum photosynthesis to occur
options.B: To ensure all stored starch is used up, giving a clear negative control
options.C: To make the leaves lose their chlorophyll
options.D: To allow the guard cells to open fully

items.explanation: Keeping the plant in the dark for 3 days ensures all pre-existing starch in the leaves is consumed through respiration. This "de-starches" the plant, so that any starch found at the end of the experiment is only due to photosynthesis during the experimental period. This gives a clean baseline for comparison.

items.question: Carbon dioxide enters a leaf through the stomata. Which factor causes the guard cells to CLOSE the stomata?

options.A: High concentration of CO2 inside the leaf
options.C: Water deficiency causing guard cells to become flaccid

items.explanation: Guard cells close stomata when they lose water and become flaccid. This happens under water-stress conditions to prevent excess transpiration. High light intensity generally opens stomata. High CO2 actually triggers closing in some plants, but the primary mechanism described in this chapter is water loss causing flaccidity.

items.question: Desert plants take up CO2 at night and prepare an intermediate. During the day they use this intermediate for photosynthesis. What advantage does this adaptation provide?

options.B: They can keep stomata closed during hot days, reducing water loss while still having CO2 for photosynthesis
options.C: They can grow faster than other plants

items.explanation: By fixing CO2 at night (when it is cooler and water loss is less), desert plants can keep their stomata closed during hot dry days to minimise water loss, while still having stored CO2 for photosynthesis driven by daytime sunlight. This is the CAM (Crassulacean Acid Metabolism) adaptation, though not named in this chapter.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Heterotrophic nutrition is the mode of nutrition in which organisms cannot synthesise their own food and therefore depend on other organisms (directly or indirectly) for complex organic food material.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: HETEROTROPHIC means "other-feeding" (hetero = other; trophe = nourishment).
Heterotrophs include animals, fungi, most bacteria, and some parasitic plants.
The strategy for obtaining food depends on whether food source is stationary (grass) or mobile (deer), and on the body design.
Some organisms break down food outside their body then absorb (fungi - SAPROTROPHIC).
Some take food in whole and break it inside (animals - HOLOZOIC).
Some derive nutrition from a living host (PARASITIC): cuscuta (amar-bel), ticks, lice, leeches, tapeworms.
All heterotrophs depend directly or indirectly on autotrophs.

items.question: What is heterotrophic nutrition? Give two examples of heterotrophic organisms.
items.answer: Heterotrophic nutrition is the mode of nutrition in which organisms cannot prepare their own food and instead depend on organic material prepared by other organisms. Examples: (1) Human beings - ingest and digest complex food. (2) Fungi (e.g., bread mould) - break down dead organic matter externally and absorb it.

items.question: Differentiate between saprotrophic and parasitic modes of heterotrophic nutrition with examples.
items.answer:
SAPROTROPHIC NUTRITION:
- Organisms break down dead and decaying organic material outside their body using enzymes, then absorb the simpler molecules.
- Examples: Fungi (yeast, bread mould, mushrooms), some bacteria.
- Host is non-living (dead organic matter).
PARASITIC NUTRITION:
- Organisms derive nutrition from the body of a living host organism, often causing harm to the host.
- Examples: Cuscuta (amar-bel) on host plants; ticks, lice on animals; tapeworms in intestines.
- Host is living and is harmed (deprived of nutrients).

items.question: Why do all heterotrophs ultimately depend on autotrophs? Explain with examples.
items.answer:
Heterotrophs cannot produce their own food from inorganic sources. All organic food ultimately originates from autotrophs (primarily green plants) through photosynthesis.
- HERBIVORES (e.g., cows, rabbits) directly eat plants - direct dependence.
- CARNIVORES (e.g., lions, tigers) eat herbivores - indirect dependence on autotrophs.
- OMNIVORES (e.g., humans) eat both plants and animals.
- PARASITES (e.g., cuscuta) directly parasitize plants or animals that ate plants.
- SAPROTROPHS (e.g., fungi) decompose plant or animal remains.
In every food chain, the first link is always an autotroph (producer). Without autotrophs, there would be no organic food for any heterotroph to consume. This is why autotrophs are called PRODUCERS and form the base of all food chains and webs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Cuscuta (amar-bel) is an example of which type of heterotrophic nutrition?
items.explanation: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant that wraps around a host plant and absorbs nutrients from it, harming the host. It cannot make its own food (not autotrophic) and does not feed on dead matter (not saprotrophic). Holozoic means ingesting whole food.

items.question: Bread mould (Rhizopus) obtains its nutrition by:

options.B: Breaking down and absorbing dead organic material (saprotrophic)

items.explanation: Bread mould is a saprotroph - it secretes enzymes onto dead organic material (bread), breaks it down externally, and then absorbs the simpler molecules. It cannot photosynthesize (no chlorophyll). Bread cells are not living when the mould grows on bread. It does not ingest whole particles.

items.question: In which type of nutrition does the organism take food into its body and digest it internally?
items.explanation: Holozoic nutrition involves ingestion (taking food into the body), internal digestion by enzymes, absorption of digested food, and egestion of waste. Examples: Amoeba, human beings. Saprotrophs digest food externally. Parasites absorb from host. Autotrophs make their own food.

items.question: Which of the following is an example of a heterotrophic organism directly depending on autotrophs?
items.explanation: A cow eating grass directly depends on autotrophs (grass = plants = autotrophs). A lion eating a deer is indirect dependence (deer ate grass). Mushroom depends on dead organic matter. A tapeworm depends on the human host who may or may not have directly eaten plants.

items.question: If all autotrophs on Earth suddenly disappeared, what would be the consequence for heterotrophs?

options.A: Heterotrophs would switch to autotrophic nutrition
options.B: Only carnivores would survive since they eat other animals
options.C: All heterotrophs would eventually die as the organic food supply would be exhausted
options.D: Saprotrophs would survive indefinitely on dead matter

items.explanation: All organic food ultimately originates from autotrophs. Without new autotrophic production, existing food stores would be consumed, dead organic matter would also eventually be exhausted by saprotrophs and decomposers, and no new organic matter would be produced. All food chains collapse at the producer level. Even carnivores depend on herbivores that ate plants. Eventually all heterotrophs would die.

subtopics.subtopic_name: HOW DO ORGANISMS OBTAIN THEIR NUTRITION?

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The mechanism by which organisms obtain nutrition varies based on their body complexity. In single-celled organisms, food is obtained over the entire body surface. In complex multicellular organisms, specialised digestive organs and systems have evolved for food intake, processing, and absorption.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: SINGLE-CELLED ORGANISMS (e.g., Amoeba): The entire cell surface is in contact with food. Amoeba uses temporary finger-like extensions called PSEUDOPODIA to engulf food particles forming a FOOD VACUOLE. Complex substances are broken down inside the vacuole; simpler molecules diffuse into cytoplasm; remaining undigested material is expelled.
PARAMOECIUM: Also unicellular; has a definite shape; food (micro-organisms) is moved to a specific spot (cytostome) by cilia covering the entire surface.
As body complexity increases, different body parts become specialised for different functions: intake, digestion, absorption, egestion.
The extent of specialisation depends on body size, body design, and energy requirements.
FIGURE 5.5: Nutrition in Amoeba - shows (a) food particle near Amoeba, (b) pseudopodia forming, (c) food vacuole forming, (d) digestion inside vacuole.

items.question: How does Amoeba obtain its nutrition?
items.answer: Amoeba is a unicellular organism that takes in food using HOLOZOIC nutrition. It extends temporary finger-like projections of its cell body called PSEUDOPODIA that fuse over the food particle (e.g., bacteria, algae) to form a FOOD VACUOLE. Inside the food vacuole, digestive enzymes break down complex food into simpler molecules which diffuse into the cytoplasm. The remaining undigested material is expelled to the surface of the cell.

items.question: How does the method of obtaining nutrition change as the complexity of an organism increases? Use examples.
items.answer:
In SIMPLE/SINGLE-CELLED ORGANISMS: The entire cell surface is in contact with the environment. Amoeba uses pseudopodia to engulf food; Paramoecium uses cilia to sweep food to a fixed spot. No specialised organs needed since the cell surface handles nutrition.
In COMPLEX MULTICELLULAR ORGANISMS: All cells are not in contact with food. Specialised organs develop:
- Mouth (intake), oesophagus (transport), stomach (partial digestion), small intestine (complete digestion + absorption), large intestine (water absorption), anus (egestion).
- Accessory organs: salivary glands, liver, pancreas.
The degree of specialisation increases with body size and energy requirements.

items.question: Describe how food is digested in Amoeba, step by step.
items.answer:
STEP 1 - INGESTION: When food (bacteria, algae) is near Amoeba, it extends PSEUDOPODIA (temporary finger-like projections of cytoplasm) which engulf the food particle.
STEP 2 - FOOD VACUOLE FORMATION: The pseudopodia fuse around the food particle, enclosing it in a membrane-bound sac called a FOOD VACUOLE. This is similar to a temporary stomach.
STEP 3 - DIGESTION: Digestive enzymes from the cytoplasm enter the food vacuole. These enzymes break down complex food molecules (proteins, carbohydrates) into simpler molecules (amino acids, glucose).
STEP 4 - ABSORPTION: The simpler molecules produced diffuse out of the food vacuole into the cytoplasm where they are used for energy and building cell components.
STEP 5 - EGESTION: The remaining undigested material is moved to the surface of the cell and thrown out (expelled) into the environment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The temporary finger-like extensions used by Amoeba to capture food are called:
items.explanation: Amoeba uses pseudopodia ("false feet") - temporary cytoplasmic projections - to engulf food. Cilia are used by Paramoecium to sweep food. Flagella are used for movement in some microorganisms. Tentacles are found in animals like Hydra, not Amoeba.

items.question: In Amoeba, where does digestion of food take place?
items.explanation: Once food is engulfed, it is enclosed in a FOOD VACUOLE. Digestive enzymes from the cytoplasm enter this vacuole and break down complex food. After digestion, simple molecules diffuse into the cytoplasm. The nucleus does not perform digestion; cell membrane is for structure.

items.question: How does Paramoecium differ from Amoeba in the way it obtains food?

options.A: Paramoecium uses pseudopodia while Amoeba uses cilia
options.B: Paramoecium has a definite shape and uses cilia to direct food to a specific spot; Amoeba uses pseudopodia
options.C: Paramoecium performs photosynthesis while Amoeba does not
options.D: Both use exactly the same method

items.explanation: Paramoecium has a definite shape (unlike Amoeba which changes shape). Paramoecium uses cilia (hair-like structures covering its surface) to sweep food to a specific entry point. Amoeba uses pseudopodia (temporary projections) to engulf food. Neither performs photosynthesis.

items.question: Why do complex multicellular organisms need specialised organs for obtaining nutrition, unlike single-celled organisms?

options.A: Single-celled organisms do not need food
options.B: In multicellular organisms, not all cells are in contact with food, requiring organs for intake, digestion, and distribution
options.C: Multicellular organisms are larger, so they need more types of food

items.explanation: In single-celled organisms, the entire cell surface is in contact with the environment, making direct absorption possible. In multicellular organisms, inner cells are not in contact with food sources, so specialised organs (mouth, stomach, intestine) are needed to process food, and a transport system is needed to deliver nutrients to all cells.

items.question: After digestion in the food vacuole of Amoeba, what happens to the remaining undigested material?

options.A: It is stored in the vacuole permanently
options.B: It is transferred to the nucleus for recycling
options.D: It is expelled to the outside of the cell

items.explanation: After absorption of digested molecules, the remaining undigested material in the food vacuole is moved to the surface of the Amoeba cell and expelled (egested) into the environment. Only the digested, simpler molecules diffuse into the cytoplasm. Nothing is stored permanently or transferred to the nucleus.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Nutrition in human beings involves the HOLOZOIC mode - ingestion of food through the mouth, digestion along the alimentary canal, absorption of nutrients in the small intestine, and egestion of undigested waste through the anus.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: ALIMENTARY CANAL: A long tube from MOUTH to ANUS. Different regions are specialised for different functions.
PERISTALSIS: Rhythmic muscular contractions of the canal wall that push food forward along the gut.
Regions and their functions:
MOUTH (BUCCAL CAVITY): Teeth crush food; tongue mixes with SALIVA (from salivary glands). Saliva contains SALIVARY AMYLASE which begins starch digestion.
OESOPHAGUS (FOOD PIPE): Connects mouth to stomach; food moves by peristalsis.
STOMACH: Muscular sac; gastric glands in wall secrete GASTRIC JUICE (HCl + PEPSIN + MUCUS). HCl creates acidic medium; Pepsin (protein-digesting enzyme) is activated; Mucus protects stomach lining.

SMALL INTESTINE: Longest part; receives BILE (from liver via gall bladder) and PANCREATIC JUICE (from pancreas). Bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice contains trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats), amylase (carbohydrates). Intestinal glands secrete intestinal juice for complete digestion.
ABSORPTION: VILLI (finger-like projections lining small intestine) absorb digested food into blood.
LARGE INTESTINE (COLON): Absorbs remaining water from undigested food.
ANUS: Egestion of waste (faeces).
SPHINCTER MUSCLE: Regulates passage of food from stomach to small intestine.
Length of small intestine varies with diet: herbivores (eating cellulose) have longer intestine; carnivores have shorter.
"DENTAL CARIES": Tooth decay - bacteria on sugars produce acids that demineralise enamel.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.3 (p.43):
sections.aim: To demonstrate the action of saliva on starch.
sections.materials: 1 mL starch solution (1%), 2 test tubes (A and B), 1 mL saliva, dilute iodine solution.
procedure: - Add 1 mL starch solution to each test tube A and B.
- Add 1 mL saliva to test tube A; leave both undisturbed for 20-30 minutes.
- Add a few drops of dilute iodine solution to both test tubes.
sections.observation: Test tube B (no saliva): turns blue-black (starch present). Test tube A (with saliva): no blue-black colour (starch absent - digested by salivary amylase).
sections.conclusion: Saliva (salivary amylase) digests starch; this shows the action of saliva on starch.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (More to Know - p.44):
sections.text:
DENTAL CARIES: Tooth decay caused by bacteria acting on sugars, producing acids that soften enamel and dentine. Masses of bacterial cells with food particles form DENTAL PLAQUE. Saliva cannot reach beneath plaque to neutralise acid. Brushing after eating removes plaque before bacteria produce acids. If untreated, microorganisms may invade the pulp, causing inflammation and infection.

items.question: What is peristalsis? What is its role in digestion?
items.answer: Peristalsis is the rhythmic, wave-like muscular contractions of the wall of the alimentary canal. The muscles contract and relax in a coordinated manner to push food forward along the digestive tube in a regulated manner, ensuring food is processed properly at each part of the canal.

items.question: What is the role of mucus in the stomach?
items.answer: The stomach secretes mucus as part of gastric juice. Mucus forms a protective lining over the inner wall of the stomach, protecting it from the corrosive action of HCl and the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin. Without mucus, the stomach would digest its own lining, causing ulcers.

items.question: Describe the digestion that takes place in the stomach.
items.answer:
The stomach is a muscular sac that receives food from the oesophagus. Three secretions from gastric glands:
(i) HYDROCHLORIC ACID (HCl): Creates a strongly acidic medium (pH ~2). This activates the enzyme pepsin, kills harmful bacteria in food, and begins some chemical breakdown of food.
(ii) PEPSIN: A protein-digesting enzyme that works in the acidic medium. It breaks proteins into smaller peptide chains.
(iii) MUCUS: Protects the inner stomach wall from HCl and pepsin.
The muscular walls churn the food, mixing it thoroughly with gastric juice. Food leaves the stomach through a SPHINCTER MUSCLE into the small intestine in small amounts at a time.

items.question: Describe the digestion and absorption that occurs in the small intestine.
items.answer:
The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption:
DIGESTION:
(i) BILE (from liver, stored in gall bladder): Makes food alkaline (neutralises stomach acid); emulsifies fats (breaks large fat globules into smaller ones for easier enzyme action).
(ii) PANCREATIC JUICE: Contains trypsin (digests proteins --> amino acids), lipase (digests fats --> fatty acids + glycerol), amylase (digests carbohydrates --> glucose).
(iii) INTESTINAL JUICE: Secreted by intestinal glands; enzymes complete the digestion of all three food types into their final absorbable forms: glucose (carbohydrates), amino acids (proteins), fatty acids + glycerol (fats).
ABSORPTION:
- The inner lining has numerous finger-like projections called VILLI which increase surface area enormously.
- Villi are richly supplied with blood vessels.
- Digested food (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol) is absorbed through villi into the blood and lymph, and transported to all cells of the body.

items.question: Trace the journey of a protein molecule from your mouth to absorption in the small intestine.
items.answer:
(i) MOUTH: Teeth mechanically break protein-containing food into small pieces. Salivary amylase acts on starch only; proteins are not digested here. Food is mixed with saliva and pushed to oesophagus.
(ii) OESOPHAGUS: No digestion; peristaltic contractions push food to stomach.
(iii) STOMACH: Gastric glands secrete HCl which activates PEPSIN. Pepsin (protein-digesting enzyme) partially breaks proteins into smaller peptide chains. Muscular churning mixes food with gastric juice.
(iv) SMALL INTESTINE - DIGESTION: (a) Bile (from liver) makes food alkaline for enzyme action. (b) Pancreatic TRYPSIN further breaks peptides into smaller units. (c) Intestinal juice enzymes (peptidases) complete the breakdown of peptide chains into individual AMINO ACIDS.
(v) SMALL INTESTINE - ABSORPTION: Amino acids (final products of protein digestion) are absorbed through VILLI into blood capillaries and transported via the hepatic portal vein to the liver, then to all body cells for protein synthesis and energy.

items.question: Write a detailed account of nutrition in human beings, covering all organs of the alimentary canal and their functions.
items.answer:
Human beings are holozoic organisms with a complete alimentary canal (digestive tube) from mouth to anus.
(i) MOUTH (BUCCAL CAVITY): Teeth mechanically break food. Salivary glands secrete SALIVA containing SALIVARY AMYLASE which begins starch digestion (starch --> maltose). Tongue mixes food with saliva, forming a bolus.
(ii) OESOPHAGUS (FOOD PIPE): No digestion. PERISTALSIS (muscular contractions) moves food to stomach.
(iii) STOMACH: A muscular, expandable sac. Gastric glands secrete GASTRIC JUICE: HCl (creates acidic medium, activates pepsin, kills bacteria), PEPSIN (digests proteins --> peptides), MUCUS (protects stomach wall). Muscular churning mixes food into chyme. SPHINCTER MUSCLE regulates entry into small intestine.
(iv) SMALL INTESTINE: The longest part (~6 m). Complete digestion occurs here.
- LIVER secretes BILE (stored in gall bladder): neutralises acid, emulsifies fats.
- PANCREAS secretes PANCREATIC JUICE: trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats), amylase (carbohydrates).
- INTESTINAL GLANDS secrete INTESTINAL JUICE: completes all digestion.
Final products: Glucose (carbs), Amino acids (proteins), Fatty acids + Glycerol (fats).
Absorption: VILLI (finger-like projections with rich blood supply) absorb all nutrients into blood; transported to cells.
(v) LARGE INTESTINE (COLON): Absorbs remaining water from undigested food.
(vi) ANUS: Undigested waste (faeces) is eliminated by the anal sphincter.
ACCESSORY ORGANS: Salivary glands, liver, gall bladder, pancreas - essential for secreting digestive juices but food does not pass through them directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The finger-like projections in the small intestine that increase surface area for absorption are called:
items.explanation: VILLI are the finger-like projections lining the small intestine that enormously increase the surface area for absorption of digested food into the blood. Cilia are hair-like structures for movement. Pseudopodia are Amoeba's food-capturing extensions. Stomata are plant leaf pores.

items.question: Gastric juice in the stomach contains:
items.explanation: Gastric juice consists of HCl (creates acidic medium), pepsin (protein-digesting enzyme), and mucus (protects stomach lining). Salivary amylase is in saliva (mouth). Bile comes from the liver. Trypsin and lipase are in pancreatic juice.

items.question: Which organ stores bile produced by the liver?
items.explanation: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the GALL BLADDER. From there, it passes into the small intestine through the bile duct when needed for fat digestion/emulsification. The pancreas produces pancreatic juice. Kidneys filter blood.

items.question: Why does the small intestine of a herbivore tend to be longer than that of a carnivore?

options.B: Cellulose (in plant food) is harder to digest and needs more time and surface area; longer intestine provides this
options.C: Carnivores have more powerful digestive enzymes
options.D: Herbivores need to absorb more water

items.explanation: Plant food contains cellulose which is difficult to digest. A longer small intestine provides more surface area and more time for digestion and absorption of plant-based food. Meat (carnivore diet) has no cellulose and is easier to digest, requiring a shorter intestine. Animal size is not the primary factor here.

items.question: In Activity 5.3, test tube A (starch + saliva) showed no blue-black colour with iodine, while test tube B (starch alone) showed blue-black. What does this prove?

options.B: Saliva contains an enzyme (salivary amylase) that digests starch
options.C: Starch is broken down by water alone

items.explanation: The blue-black colour indicates the presence of starch. Its absence in tube A (with saliva) means the starch has been digested. Since the only variable is the presence of saliva (which contains salivary amylase), the enzyme in saliva is responsible for starch digestion. Iodine does not react with saliva. Water alone (tube B) did not digest starch.

items.question: What is the role of HCl in the stomach?

options.B: It activates pepsin and creates an acidic medium for protein digestion
options.C: It neutralises bile from the liver
options.D: It absorbs nutrients into the blood

items.explanation: HCl in gastric juice creates a strongly acidic medium (pH ~2) which is needed to activate the protein-digesting enzyme PEPSIN (which is secreted as inactive pepsinogen). HCl also kills many harmful microorganisms in food. It does not digest fats directly (that is bile + lipase), does not neutralise bile (bile is alkaline and it is the pancreatic juice that neutralises the acid), and does not absorb nutrients.

items.question: If the gall bladder is surgically removed, what effect would this most likely have on digestion?

options.C: Fat digestion would be less efficient since bile cannot be stored and released in concentrated bursts
options.D: The stomach would produce more acid

items.explanation: Bile produced by the liver emulsifies fats (breaks fat globules into smaller droplets). The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile, releasing it in a controlled manner when fat-containing food enters the small intestine. Without the gall bladder, bile drips continuously from the liver in smaller amounts, reducing efficiency of fat emulsification. Protein digestion (pepsin, trypsin) and starch digestion (amylase) are not affected by bile. Stomach acid production is independent.

items.question: A student consumes a meal rich in proteins, carbohydrates, and fats. Arrange the following digestive events in the CORRECT sequence: 1. Bile emulsifies fats in small intestine 2. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in mouth 3. Pepsin digests proteins in stomach 4. Villi absorb amino acids, glucose, fatty acids into blood
items.explanation: Correct sequence: (2) Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the MOUTH first. Then (3) Pepsin acts on proteins in the STOMACH. Then (1) Bile emulsifies fats in the SMALL INTESTINE. Finally (4) Villi absorb the completely digested nutrients (amino acids, glucose, fatty acids) in the SMALL INTESTINE. This follows the anatomical order: mouth --> stomach --> small intestine.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Respiration is the biological process by which living organisms break down food (glucose) to release energy for cellular activities. The process involves the transfer of energy into ATP molecules.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: All living cells carry out respiration to obtain energy.
FIRST STEP (common to all organisms): Breakdown of glucose (6-carbon) into PYRUVATE (3-carbon) in the CYTOPLASM. This releases some energy.
AEROBIC RESPIRATION: Pyruvate is broken down in the MITOCHONDRIA using oxygen. Products: CO2 + H2O + large amount of energy (ATP).
ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION: Pyruvate is broken down without oxygen.
In YEAST (fermentation): Pyruvate --> Ethanol + CO2 + Energy.
In MUSCLE CELLS (during sudden activity/lack of O2): Pyruvate --> Lactic acid + Energy. Build-up of lactic acid causes muscle cramps.
Aerobic respiration releases far more energy than anaerobic.
Overall equation (aerobic): C6H12O6 + 6O2 --> 6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy (ATP).
ATP is the universal energy currency; used for all cellular activities.
HAEMOGLOBIN in red blood cells transports O2; has very high affinity for oxygen.
CO2 is more soluble in water than O2; transported mostly in dissolved form in blood.
IN PLANTS: Gas exchange via STOMATA (leaves, stems). Intercellular air spaces ensure all cells contact air.
IN HUMAN BEINGS: Air enters through nostrils --> pharynx --> larynx --> trachea (ringed by cartilage) --> bronchi --> bronchioles --> ALVEOLI (air sacs in lungs).
ALVEOLI: Balloon-like structures; thin walls; extensive blood vessel network; provide enormous surface area (~80 m2 if spread out) for gas exchange.
Breathing mechanism: inhaling lifts ribs and flattens diaphragm, expanding chest cavity; air is sucked in. Exhaling reverses this.
Lungs always contain a RESIDUAL VOLUME of air to allow continuous gas exchange.
RESPIRATORY PIGMENT: Haemoglobin in red blood cells takes up oxygen in lungs; releases at tissues.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.4 (p.45):
sections.aim: To show that exhaled air contains CO2.
sections.materials: Test tube with freshly prepared lime water, rubber tube, pichkari/syringe.
procedure: - (a) Use pichkari to pass air through lime water. Note time for lime water to turn milky.
- (b) Exhale through a tube into lime water. Note time for lime water to turn milky.
sections.observation: Lime water turns milky more quickly with exhaled air than with atmospheric air.
sections.conclusion: Exhaled air contains more CO2 than inhaled air. CO2 turns lime water milky (calcium carbonate precipitate).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.5 (p.45):
sections.aim: To demonstrate anaerobic respiration (fermentation) by yeast.
sections.materials: Fruit juice or sugar solution, yeast, test tube with one-holed cork, bent glass tube, fresh lime water.
procedure: - Add yeast to fruit juice/sugar solution in test tube; fit cork with bent glass tube; dip free end into lime water.
sections.observation: Lime water turns milky; time taken is longer than for exhaled air.
sections.conclusion: Yeast produces CO2 during anaerobic respiration (fermentation). CO2 production indicates fermentation is occurring.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.6 (p.47):
sections.aim: To observe breathing rate in fish.
procedure: Observe fish in aquarium - count the number of times the fish opens and closes its mouth per minute. Compare with human breathing rate.
sections.conclusion: Dissolved oxygen in water is much less than O2 in air; aquatic organisms must breathe faster to obtain sufficient oxygen. This shows the advantage terrestrial organisms have in obtaining O2.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS:
sections.text: MORE TO KNOW (p.47): Tobacco and its products (cigars, cigarettes, bidis, hookah, gutkha) are harmful. Most commonly affects tongue, lungs, heart, and liver. Smokeless tobacco is a risk factor for heart attacks, strokes, pulmonary diseases, and cancers. High incidence of oral cancer in India due to tobacco chewing (gutkha). Stay healthy; say NO to tobacco.

sections.label: DO YOU KNOW? (p.48-59):
sections.text:
- If the alveolar surface were spread out, it would cover about 80 m2 - much larger than the body surface. This explains the efficiency of gas exchange.
- If oxygen diffused through the body on its own, it would take 3 years for a molecule to reach the toes from the lungs. Haemoglobin makes transport rapid.
- Smoking destroys cilia in upper respiratory tract (small hair-like structures that remove germs, dust, harmful particles), allowing them to enter lungs causing infection, cough, lung cancer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?
items.answer: BREATHING is a physical process - the mechanical movement of air in and out of the lungs (inhalation and exhalation). RESPIRATION is a biochemical process that occurs at the cellular level - the breakdown of glucose using oxygen to produce ATP (energy). Breathing supplies oxygen for respiration; respiration is the actual energy-releasing process.

items.question: Why do aquatic organisms have a higher breathing rate than terrestrial organisms?
items.answer: Dissolved oxygen in water is far less than oxygen present in the atmosphere. To obtain sufficient oxygen for respiration, aquatic organisms must take in water at a much faster rate and pass it over their gills more frequently. Hence their breathing rate is much higher than that of terrestrial organisms who breathe oxygen-rich air.

items.question: Describe the three pathways of glucose breakdown in different organisms.
items.answer:
The breakdown of glucose (6-carbon) begins in the cytoplasm with glycolysis, forming PYRUVATE (3-carbon). From pyruvate, three pathways are possible:
(i) IN YEAST (absence of oxygen): Pyruvate --> Ethanol (2-carbon) + Carbon dioxide + Energy. This is ANAEROBIC FERMENTATION. The energy released is relatively less.
(ii) IN MUSCLE CELLS (lack of oxygen): Pyruvate --> Lactic acid (3-carbon) + Energy. This ANAEROBIC pathway occurs during sudden activity. Build-up of lactic acid causes muscle cramps.
(iii) IN AEROBIC ORGANISMS (presence of oxygen): Pyruvate enters MITOCHONDRIA; broken down using O2 into Carbon dioxide + Water + large amount of Energy (ATP). This is AEROBIC RESPIRATION - releases far more energy than anaerobic.

items.question: Describe the structure and functioning of the human respiratory system.
items.answer:
The human respiratory system:
STRUCTURE:
- Air enters through NOSTRILS; fine hairs filter dust; mucus traps particles.
- PHARYNX --> LARYNX --> TRACHEA: Trachea has rings of cartilage to keep it from collapsing.
- BRONCHI: Trachea divides into two bronchi (one for each lung).
- BRONCHIOLES: Bronchi divide into smaller bronchioles.
- ALVEOLI: Bronchioles end in balloon-like AIR SACS called alveoli. Walls of alveoli are very thin (one cell thick); covered with a dense network of blood capillaries. The alveolar surface area (if spread out) is ~80 m2, providing enormous area for gas exchange.
FUNCTIONING:
- Breathing in: Ribs lift up, diaphragm flattens --> chest cavity expands --> air is sucked into lungs.
- Gas exchange: Oxygen from alveolar air diffuses into blood; CO2 from blood diffuses into alveoli.
- Haemoglobin in red blood cells carries O2 to all tissues; CO2 is transported mainly dissolved in blood plasma.
- Breathing out: Ribs move in, diaphragm rises --> chest cavity reduces --> air is pushed out.
- A residual volume of air always stays in lungs to ensure continuous gas exchange.

items.question: How is oxygen transported in the blood? Why is haemoglobin important?
items.answer:
OXYGEN TRANSPORT:
- Oxygen absorbed in alveoli is picked up by HAEMOGLOBIN, a respiratory pigment present in RED BLOOD CORPUSCLES.
- Haemoglobin has a very HIGH AFFINITY for oxygen - it combines readily with O2 in the oxygen-rich alveolar environment to form oxyhaemoglobin.
- Oxyhaemoglobin is transported in blood to all tissues.
- At tissues where oxygen levels are low, haemoglobin releases oxygen (oxyhaemoglobin dissociates), and oxygen diffuses into cells for respiration.
IMPORTANCE OF HAEMOGLOBIN:
- Without haemoglobin, oxygen would have to diffuse through body fluids on its own, taking approximately 3 YEARS to reach the toes from the lungs.
- Haemoglobin makes oxygen transport efficient, rapid, and reliable.
CARBON DIOXIDE TRANSPORT:
- CO2 is more soluble in water than O2.
- CO2 is transported mainly in the DISSOLVED FORM in blood plasma (not by haemoglobin primarily).

items.question: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Include the location, raw materials, products, and relative energy yield.
items.answer:
AEROBIC RESPIRATION:
- LOCATION: Starts in cytoplasm (glycolysis), continues in MITOCHONDRIA.
- RAW MATERIALS: Glucose + Oxygen.
- PRODUCTS: Carbon dioxide + Water + Large amount of Energy (ATP).
- EQUATION: C6H12O6 + 6O2 --> 6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy.
- ENERGY YIELD: Very high (38 ATP molecules per glucose molecule).
- EXAMPLES: Humans, most animals and plants, aerobic bacteria.

ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION:
- LOCATION: CYTOPLASM only (no mitochondria involvement for final products).
- RAW MATERIALS: Glucose only (NO oxygen).
(a) IN YEAST: Glucose --> Ethanol + CO2 + Small amount of Energy. Used industrially for fermentation (bread, beer, wine).
(b) IN MUSCLE CELLS: Glucose --> Lactic Acid + Small amount of Energy. Causes muscle cramps due to lactic acid build-up.
- ENERGY YIELD: Low (2 ATP molecules per glucose).

COMPARISON:
Feature - Aerobic - Anaerobic
Oxygen required - Yes - No
Location - Cytoplasm + Mitochondria - Cytoplasm only
Carbon products - CO2 - CO2 (yeast) / Lactic acid (muscles)
Energy released - High (38 ATP) - Low (2 ATP)
Examples - Humans, plants - Yeast, muscle cells (temporary)

NOTE: Aerobic respiration is preferred by organisms as it is much more efficient. Anaerobic respiration in muscles is temporary (during sudden activity); the lactic acid is later oxidised when oxygen becomes available.

items.question: Where in the cell does the first step of glucose breakdown (glycolysis) occur?
items.explanation: Glycolysis - the breakdown of glucose (6-carbon) into pyruvate (3-carbon) - occurs in the CYTOPLASM of all cells. This is the first step common to both aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Mitochondria are involved in the subsequent aerobic breakdown of pyruvate.

items.question: When yeast ferments sugar in the absence of oxygen, the products are:
items.explanation: Yeast performs anaerobic respiration (fermentation): Pyruvate --> Ethanol + CO2 + Energy. Lactic acid is produced in muscle cells (not yeast). CO2 + water + large energy is from aerobic respiration. Glucose and oxygen are reactants, not products.

items.question: The rings of cartilage in the trachea serve which function?

options.B: To prevent the trachea from collapsing when air pressure changes during breathing

items.explanation: Rings of cartilage around the trachea keep it rigid and prevent it from collapsing during inhalation when air pressure inside drops. Sound is produced by the larynx (voice box). Nasal hairs and mucus filter dust. Blood vessels in the nasal passage warm incoming air.

items.question: Build-up of which substance in muscle cells causes cramps during sudden strenuous exercise?
items.explanation: During sudden vigorous exercise, oxygen supply to muscles is insufficient. Muscles resort to anaerobic respiration: Pyruvate --> LACTIC ACID + Energy. Accumulation of lactic acid in muscles causes the painful sensation of cramps. Ethanol is produced by yeast. Pyruvate is an intermediate. CO2 does not cause cramps.

items.question: Why do aerobic organisms need to ensure sufficient oxygen intake?

options.A: Oxygen is needed to produce glucose
options.B: The aerobic respiration pathway in mitochondria depends on oxygen to completely break down pyruvate and release maximum energy
options.C: Oxygen is needed to manufacture haemoglobin
options.D: Oxygen prevents lactic acid formation in all organisms

items.explanation: Aerobic respiration in mitochondria uses oxygen to completely oxidise pyruvate (from glycolysis) to CO2 and water, releasing a large amount of energy (38 ATP). Without sufficient oxygen, only anaerobic respiration occurs, producing only 2 ATP - far less efficient. Oxygen is not needed to produce glucose (that comes from food). Haemoglobin production does not require oxygen. Lactic acid formation is specific to muscle cells, not all organisms.

items.question: Which process is shown in Activity 5.5 (yeast + sugar solution releasing CO2 into lime water)?
items.explanation: The set-up in Activity 5.5 has no oxygen (closed container with yeast and sugar solution). Yeast performs ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION (fermentation), producing CO2 that turns lime water milky. If oxygen were present, aerobic respiration would give more CO2 more quickly. Photosynthesis requires light and produces oxygen. Transpiration involves water vapour, not CO2.

items.question: A patient has a deficiency of haemoglobin (anaemia). Which of the following would be the MOST direct consequence?

options.B: Insufficient oxygen delivery to body tissues, causing fatigue
options.C: Inability to excrete carbon dioxide from the body
options.D: Failure of glucose breakdown in the cytoplasm

items.explanation: Haemoglobin in red blood cells is the primary carrier of oxygen from lungs to tissues. A deficiency means less oxygen is transported to tissues, impairing aerobic respiration in cells and causing fatigue, weakness, and breathlessness. CO2 is transported mostly dissolved in plasma (not haemoglobin). Digestion and glycolysis do not directly depend on haemoglobin.

items.question: In a plant at night (no photosynthesis), what is the NET gas exchange at the stomata?

options.A: Only CO2 is released; no O2 exchange
options.B: CO2 is released (from respiration) and O2 is absorbed (for respiration)
options.C: O2 is released and CO2 is absorbed
options.D: No gas exchange occurs at night

items.explanation: At night, photosynthesis stops (no light). Respiration continues - cells break down glucose using O2 and release CO2. Since there is no photosynthesis to consume CO2 or produce O2, the NET exchange at night is: CO2 is released out and O2 is absorbed in. During the day, photosynthesis consumes all the CO2 produced by respiration (and more), so there appears to be no net CO2 release; oxygen is the major event.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Transportation is the life process by which materials (food, oxygen, water, minerals, waste products) are moved from one part of the organism to another to reach all cells for use or removal.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: In single-celled organisms, diffusion suffices. In multicellular organisms, specialised transport systems are needed.
In HUMAN BEINGS: Circulatory system - HEART (pump) + BLOOD (fluid) + BLOOD VESSELS (arteries, veins, capillaries) + LYMPHATIC SYSTEM.
In PLANTS: XYLEM transports water and minerals (from roots upward). PHLOEM transports food/photosynthetic products (from leaves to all parts - upward and downward).
LYMPH is a colourless fluid similar to plasma, formed by leakage from capillaries into intercellular spaces; drains back into blood via lymph vessels. Carries digested fat from intestine.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.7 (p.49):
sections.aim: To find out the normal range of haemoglobin content in human beings.
procedure: Visit a health centre/veterinary clinic; find out normal haemoglobin range for men, women, children, adults; compare with animals like buffalo/cow.
sections.observation: Normal haemoglobin levels vary between males, females, children, and animals.
sections.conclusion:
Haemoglobin content is different in different groups; differences between male and female exist in both humans and animals.

items.question: What are the components of the transport system in human beings?
items.answer: The transport system in human beings consists of: (1) HEART - the muscular pump that pushes blood through the body. (2) BLOOD - the fluid that carries nutrients, oxygen, CO2, hormones, and waste products. (3) BLOOD VESSELS - arteries (carry blood from heart), veins (carry blood to heart), capillaries (thin-walled, for exchange). (4) LYMPHATIC SYSTEM - lymph capillaries and vessels that drain excess tissue fluid back to blood.

items.question: What is lymph? What is its role?
items.answer: LYMPH is a pale yellow fluid formed when some plasma, proteins, and white blood cells escape from capillaries into the intercellular spaces to form TISSUE FLUID. This fluid drains into lymphatic capillaries. Lymph is similar to blood plasma but colourless and contains less protein. Its roles: (1) Returns excess fluid from tissues to blood. (2) Carries digested and absorbed FAT from the intestine (via lacteals in villi) to blood. (3) Contains white blood cells (lymphocytes) that help fight infection.

items.question: Describe the double circulation of blood in human beings. Why is it necessary?
items.answer:
In human beings, blood passes through the heart TWICE in one complete circuit - this is called DOUBLE CIRCULATION.
(i) PULMONARY CIRCULATION: Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle is pumped to the LUNGS via pulmonary arteries. In the lungs, CO2 is released and O2 is absorbed. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium via pulmonary veins.
(ii) SYSTEMIC CIRCULATION: Oxygenated blood from the left ventricle is pumped to ALL BODY ORGANS via the aorta. Nutrients and O2 are delivered; CO2 and waste are collected. Deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium via vena cava.
NECESSITY: The SEPTUM (dividing wall) in the heart prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. This ensures a highly efficient supply of oxygen to tissues - essential for birds and mammals that use energy to maintain constant body temperature.

items.question: How are arteries, veins, and capillaries structurally different? How do these differences relate to their functions?
items.answer:
ARTERIES:
- Structure: Thick, elastic, muscular walls; no valves.
- Function: Carry blood AWAY from the heart to organs, under HIGH PRESSURE (due to heart pumping). Thick walls withstand this pressure.
VEINS:
- Structure: Thin walls; have VALVES to prevent backflow of blood.
- Function: Carry blood TOWARDS the heart from organs, under LOW PRESSURE (blood is no longer under pumping force). Valves ensure one-directional flow. Blood is returned by squeezing action of nearby muscles and gravity.
CAPILLARIES:
- Structure: ONE CELL THICK walls; smallest vessels; form dense networks in organs.
- Function: Allow EXCHANGE of materials between blood and individual cells. Their thin, porous walls allow oxygen, nutrients, and CO2 to pass in and out. They then join to form veins.

items.question: How do plants transport water from roots to leaves?
items.answer:
Water transport in plants occurs through XYLEM tissue:
(i) ROOT PRESSURE: Root cells actively absorb mineral ions from soil. This lowers the water potential in root cells, causing water from soil to enter roots by osmosis. This creates a root pressure that pushes water upwards into xylem.
(ii) TRANSPIRATION PULL (main driving force): Water evaporates from cells of leaves into air spaces and exits through stomata as water vapour (TRANSPIRATION). This loss of water from the leaf cells creates a suction/pulling force that draws water upward through the xylem from roots - the TRANSPIRATION PULL. This is the major force for water movement in tall trees.
- Xylem consists of vessels and tracheids that form a continuous water-conducting channel from roots to all parts.
- Activity 5.8 demonstrates: a plant with leaves transpires more water (plastic sheet over soil; the plant pot shows moisture condensation on the cover); a stick (no leaves = no transpiration) does not.

items.question: Compare the transport systems in human beings and in plants.
items.answer:
TRANSPORT IN HUMAN BEINGS:
(i) FLUID: Blood (contains plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets).
(ii) PUMP: HEART (4-chambered: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle).
(iii) VESSELS: Arteries (from heart), Veins (to heart), Capillaries (exchange).
(iv) TYPE: DOUBLE CIRCULATION (pulmonary + systemic). Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood kept separate.
(v) MATERIALS TRANSPORTED: Oxygen, CO2, nutrients, hormones, excretory waste.
(vi) ENERGY: Active pumping by heart; continuous circulation.
(vii) LYMPHATIC SYSTEM: Drains excess tissue fluid; returns to blood.

TRANSPORT IN PLANTS:
(i) TWO SEPARATE SYSTEMS:
(a) XYLEM: Carries water and minerals from ROOTS upwards to leaves. One-way (upward) flow. Driving force: Root pressure + Transpiration pull. Xylem cells are dead.
(b) PHLOEM: Carries food (sucrose, amino acids, etc.) from LEAVES to all parts (up and down). Requires ENERGY (ATP) for loading sucrose into phloem (translocation). Phloem cells are living (sieve tube cells + companion cells).
(ii) NO PUMP: Plants use passive forces (osmosis, transpiration pull) and active transport for phloem loading.
(iii) ENERGY NEEDS: Low (plants are non-motile; lower energy demands).

KEY DIFFERENCE: Animals have a dedicated pump (heart) driving circulation; plants rely on physical forces (transpiration, osmosis) and ATP for food translocation. Animals transport blood in vessels; plants use xylem and phloem tissues.
