items.question: Which blood vessel carries blood FROM the heart to the rest of the body?
items.explanation: The AORTA is the largest artery that carries oxygenated blood from the LEFT VENTRICLE to all parts of the body. Vena cava brings deoxygenated blood BACK to the right atrium. Pulmonary vein brings oxygenated blood from lungs to left atrium. Coronary veins drain the heart muscle itself.

items.question: Xylem in plants is responsible for transporting:

options.A: Food (photosynthetic products) from leaves to all parts
options.B: Water and minerals from roots to leaves

items.explanation: XYLEM transports water and dissolved minerals absorbed by roots upward to leaves and other parts. PHLOEM transports food (photosynthetic products like sucrose) from leaves to other parts. Oxygen transport is by diffusion through intercellular spaces, not xylem.

items.question: What is the normal blood pressure in a healthy adult?
items.explanation: Normal blood pressure is 120 mm Hg SYSTOLIC (during ventricular contraction) and 80 mm Hg DIASTOLIC (during ventricular relaxation), written as 120/80 mm Hg. Values above this (e.g., 140/100) indicate HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure).

items.question: Why is it important that the heart has a septum (dividing wall) between its left and right sides?

options.A: To make the heart beat faster
options.B: To prevent the mixing of oxygenated (left side) and deoxygenated (right side) blood, ensuring efficient oxygen delivery
options.C: To pump blood to the lungs only

items.explanation: The septum ensures complete separation of oxygenated blood (left side, from lungs) and deoxygenated blood (right side, from body). This DOUBLE CIRCULATION prevents mixing and ensures that oxygen-rich blood is always pumped to body tissues. This is especially important in birds and mammals that need efficient oxygen supply to maintain body temperature. Amphibians with 3-chambered hearts have some mixing.

items.question: What is translocation in plants?

options.A: Movement of water from roots to leaves through xylem
options.B: Transport of photosynthetic products (food) from leaves through phloem to all plant parts
options.C: Loss of water vapour from leaves

items.explanation: TRANSLOCATION is the transport of soluble products of photosynthesis (mainly sucrose) from leaves (where they are produced) through PHLOEM to all other parts of the plant (roots, stems, fruits, seeds) where they are needed. This is different from xylem transport (water/minerals). Water loss is transpiration; mineral absorption is by roots.

items.question: Platelets in the blood help in:

options.C: Clotting blood to plug leaks in damaged vessels

items.explanation: PLATELETS (thrombocytes) circulate in blood and are essential for blood clotting. When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets aggregate at the site and help form a clot to stop bleeding. Red blood cells carry oxygen. White blood cells fight infection. CO2 is mainly transported dissolved in plasma.

items.question: A plant in Activity 5.8 has its leaves covered with plastic. What happens to water transport in its xylem?

options.A: Water transport increases because roots absorb more water
options.B: Water transport slows down because transpiration (which provides the main pulling force) is stopped
options.C: Water transport is unchanged; only the roots are affected

items.explanation: The main driving force for water movement through xylem in tall plants is the TRANSPIRATION PULL - water evaporating from leaves creates suction that pulls water up. Covering leaves with plastic prevents transpiration. Without transpiration pull, the driving force for xylem transport is greatly reduced (only weak root pressure remains). Water transport slows significantly. This is why plants wilt when they lose water faster than it can be supplied.

items.question: Blood pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer. High blood pressure (hypertension) is caused by constriction of arterioles. Why does arteriole constriction raise blood pressure?

options.B: Constricted arterioles increase resistance to blood flow, causing the heart to pump harder, raising pressure
options.C: Constricted arterioles produce more blood cells
options.D: Constriction directly stimulates the heart to beat faster

items.explanation: ARTERIOLES are small arteries that regulate blood flow to capillary beds. When arterioles constrict (narrow), resistance to blood flow INCREASES. To push blood through narrowed vessels, the heart must pump with GREATER FORCE, raising the pressure in arteries. This is HYPERTENSION. Over time, high pressure can rupture vessels or lead to organ damage. Constriction does not increase blood volume or directly affect heart rate.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Transportation in human beings is carried out by the CIRCULATORY SYSTEM consisting of the heart (pump), blood (transport fluid), and blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries). Blood transports oxygen, food, hormones, CO2, and excretory waste to and from all cells.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: BLOOD: Fluid connective tissue. Contains:
PLASMA: Liquid medium (mostly water); transports food, CO2, and nitrogenous wastes in dissolved form.
RED BLOOD CORPUSCLES (RBCs): Contain HAEMOGLOBIN; carry O2.
WHITE BLOOD CELLS (WBCs): Immune function; fight pathogens.
PLATELETS: Blood clotting.
HEART: Muscular organ, size of a fist. Four chambers: Right Atrium (RA), Right Ventricle (RV), Left Atrium (LA), Left Ventricle (LV).
RA receives deoxygenated blood from body via VENA CAVA.
RV pumps it to lungs via PULMONARY ARTERIES.
LA receives oxygenated blood from lungs via PULMONARY VEINS.
LV pumps it to body via AORTA.
SEPTUM divides right and left sides preventing blood mixing.
VALVES prevent backflow between chambers and into vessels.
Ventricles have THICKER walls than atria (must pump blood to greater distances).
DOUBLE CIRCULATION: Blood goes through heart twice per complete circuit.
BLOOD PRESSURE: Force exerted by blood on vessel walls. Measured by SPHYGMOMANOMETER. Normal: 120/80 mm Hg. High blood pressure = HYPERTENSION (caused by arteriole constriction; can rupture vessels).
LYMPH: Tissue fluid in intercellular spaces; collected by lymph capillaries; returned to blood. Contains lymphocytes (immune cells). Carries absorbed fats from intestine.
MORE TO KNOW (p.61):

BLOOD PRESSURE: Force of blood against vessel walls. Pressure in arteries >> veins. Systolic pressure = pressure during ventricular contraction (normally 120 mm Hg). Diastolic pressure = pressure during relaxation (normally 80 mm Hg). Instrument: SPHYGMOMANOMETER. High blood pressure = HYPERTENSION = caused by arteriole constriction = increased resistance to blood flow = risk of artery rupture and internal bleeding.

sections.label: THINK IT OVER (p.66):
sections.text:
ORGAN DONATION: A generous act of donating an organ or tissue to a person with non-functioning organ(s). Donation can occur by consent of donor and family. Anyone regardless of age or gender can donate. Common transplants: corneas, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, intestines, bone marrow. Most donations occur after brain death but kidneys, part of liver, and lungs can be donated by living donors.

items.question: What is blood pressure? What instrument is used to measure it?
items.answer: Blood pressure is the force that blood exerts against the walls of blood vessels. It is much greater in arteries than in veins. Normal blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic). It is measured using an instrument called a SPHYGMOMANOMETER.

items.question: What is the function of valves in the heart and veins?
items.answer: VALVES ensure ONE-DIRECTIONAL flow of blood. (1) HEART VALVES: Present between atria and ventricles, and at exits of ventricles into pulmonary artery and aorta. They prevent backflow of blood when chambers contract - ensuring blood flows only in the correct direction. (2) VEIN VALVES: Present in veins to prevent backflow of blood (since blood in veins is under low pressure). They ensure blood flows only towards the heart.

items.question: Describe the four chambers of the human heart and their roles.
items.answer:
The human heart has four chambers:
(i) RIGHT ATRIUM (RA): Receives DEOXYGENATED blood from the body through the VENA CAVA (superior and inferior). When RA contracts, blood passes to the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.
(ii) RIGHT VENTRICLE (RV): Receives deoxygenated blood from RA. When RV contracts, blood is pumped to the LUNGS through the PULMONARY ARTERIES for oxygenation.
(iii) LEFT ATRIUM (LA): Receives OXYGENATED blood from the lungs through the PULMONARY VEINS. When LA contracts, blood passes to the left ventricle through the bicuspid (mitral) valve.
(iv) LEFT VENTRICLE (LV): Receives oxygenated blood from LA. When LV contracts, blood is pumped to the ENTIRE BODY through the AORTA. LV has the THICKEST walls as it must generate the highest pressure to pump blood to all parts.
The SEPTUM divides the left and right sides, preventing mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

items.question: Describe the structure and function of the three types of blood vessels.
items.answer:
Three types of blood vessels:
(i) ARTERIES:
- Structure: Thick, muscular, elastic walls; no valves; carry blood under HIGH PRESSURE.
- Function: Carry blood AWAY from the heart to organs. The aorta is the largest artery. As arteries reach organs, they divide into smaller arterioles and then capillaries.
(ii) VEINS:
- Structure: Thin walls; have VALVES at intervals; carry blood under LOW PRESSURE.
- Function: Carry blood TOWARDS the heart from organs. Vena cava (superior and inferior) are the largest veins returning blood to the right atrium.
(iii) CAPILLARIES:
- Structure: ONE CELL THICK walls (squamous epithelium); very narrow; form dense networks in organs and tissues.
- Function: Allow EXCHANGE of materials (O2, nutrients from blood to cells; CO2, waste from cells to blood) by diffusion. They connect arterioles (arterial end) to venules (venous end).

items.question: Describe double circulation in human beings. Why is it necessary for birds and mammals?
items.answer:
DOUBLE CIRCULATION: Blood completes TWO separate circuits in one full journey around the body:
(i) PULMONARY CIRCULATION:
- Deoxygenated blood: Right Atrium --> Right Ventricle --> Pulmonary Arteries --> LUNGS (CO2 released, O2 absorbed) --> Pulmonary Veins --> Left Atrium.
(ii) SYSTEMIC CIRCULATION:
- Oxygenated blood: Left Atrium --> Left Ventricle --> Aorta --> ALL BODY ORGANS (O2 + nutrients delivered, CO2 + waste collected) --> Vena Cava --> Right Atrium.
NECESSITY FOR BIRDS AND MAMMALS:
- Birds and mammals are WARM-BLOODED - they maintain a constant body temperature requiring continuous, high energy expenditure.
- This demands a highly efficient oxygen supply to all tissues.
- Double circulation with a 4-chambered heart ensures COMPLETE SEPARATION of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, maximising oxygen delivery efficiency.
- Amphibians and reptiles have 3-chambered hearts (some mixing occurs); fish have 2-chambered hearts (blood through heart once per circuit - single circulation).

items.question: Describe the composition and functions of blood.
items.answer:
Blood is a fluid connective tissue, the main transport medium in the body. It consists of a FLUID COMPONENT and CELLULAR COMPONENTS:

PLASMA (55% of blood):
- Liquid medium; mostly water (~90%).
- Transports dissolved substances: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, CO2, hormones, urea, salts.
- Contains proteins (albumin, fibrinogen for clotting, antibodies).

CELLULAR COMPONENTS (45%):
(i) RED BLOOD CORPUSCLES (RBCs / Erythrocytes):
- Most numerous blood cells (~5 million/mm3).
- Contain HAEMOGLOBIN (red protein that binds O2).
- No nucleus in mature human RBCs.
- Function: OXYGEN TRANSPORT from lungs to all tissues.

(ii) WHITE BLOOD CELLS (WBCs / Leucocytes):
- Far fewer than RBCs (~5000-10000/mm3).
- Have nuclei; several types (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, etc.).
- Function: IMMUNE DEFENCE - engulf bacteria (phagocytosis), produce antibodies, fight infections.

(iii) PLATELETS (Thrombocytes):
- Cell fragments (no nucleus).
- Function: BLOOD CLOTTING - aggregate at wound site and initiate clotting cascade to stop bleeding. Prevent excessive blood loss.

FUNCTIONS OF BLOOD AS A WHOLE:
(1) Transports O2 from lungs to cells (via haemoglobin).
(2) Transports CO2 from cells to lungs (dissolved in plasma).
(3) Transports digested food from intestine to all cells (plasma).
(4) Transports hormones from glands to target organs.
(5) Transports excretory waste (urea) from cells to kidneys.
(6) Regulates body temperature (distributes heat).
(7) Fights infections (WBCs).
(8) Prevents blood loss (platelets + clotting factors in plasma).

items.question: The muscular wall separating the left and right sides of the heart is called:
items.explanation: The SEPTUM is the muscular wall dividing the heart into left and right halves. It prevents mixing of oxygenated (left side) and deoxygenated (right side) blood. Valves prevent backflow within chambers. Aorta and vena cava are blood vessels, not heart structures.

items.question: Which component of blood is responsible for carrying oxygen?
items.explanation: RED BLOOD CORPUSCLES contain HAEMOGLOBIN, the respiratory pigment that binds oxygen and transports it from lungs to tissues. Plasma carries dissolved substances. Platelets clot blood. White blood cells fight infection.

items.question: Blood pressure is measured in:
items.explanation: Blood pressure is measured in mm Hg (millimetres of mercury) using a sphygmomanometer. The normal value is 120 mm Hg (systolic) / 80 mm Hg (diastolic). Joules is energy. Beats per minute is heart rate. Litres per minute is cardiac output.

items.question: Why do the ventricles have thicker walls than the atria?

options.A: Because the ventricles receive blood, not pump it
options.B: Because the ventricles must pump blood to the lungs and body with greater force, requiring thicker muscular walls
options.C: Because the ventricles are smaller than the atria
options.D: Because the ventricles are on the left side of the heart

items.explanation: ATRIA receive blood and pump it only to the adjacent ventricles (short distance, low pressure needed). VENTRICLES pump blood to the lungs (right ventricle) and entire body (left ventricle) - much greater distances and pressures required. Therefore ventricles have thicker, more muscular walls. The left ventricle has the thickest walls as it pumps blood farthest.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of plasma in blood?

options.C: Transport of CO2 from cells to lungs (dissolved)

items.explanation: Oxygen is carried by HAEMOGLOBIN in RED BLOOD CORPUSCLES, NOT by plasma. Plasma does transport glucose, CO2 (dissolved), urea, hormones, amino acids, and clotting factors. So option (B) - carrying oxygen - is NOT a function of plasma.

items.question: What is hypertension?

options.A: Low blood pressure caused by excess blood volume
options.B: High blood pressure caused by constriction of arterioles, increasing resistance to blood flow

items.explanation: HYPERTENSION (high blood pressure) occurs when arterioles constrict, increasing resistance to blood flow. The heart must pump harder to maintain circulation, raising pressure in arteries. Normal is 120/80 mm Hg; hypertension is typically above 140/90. It can cause rupture of arteries and internal bleeding. Low blood pressure is hypotension. Irregular heartbeat is arrhythmia. Red blood cell deficiency is anaemia.

items.question: During the pumping cycle, when does the bicuspid (mitral) valve between the left atrium and left ventricle CLOSE?

options.B: When the left ventricle contracts (to prevent blood from flowing back into the atrium)
options.C: When blood enters the left atrium from pulmonary veins

items.explanation: The BICUSPID (MITRAL) VALVE closes when the LEFT VENTRICLE CONTRACTS. As the left ventricle contracts to pump blood into the aorta, the high pressure inside would force blood backwards into the left atrium if the bicuspid valve were open. Closing the valve prevents this backflow and ensures all blood is pumped forward into the aorta. The valve opens when the left atrium contracts (to allow blood into the relaxed left ventricle).

items.question: If a person's white blood cell count is very low, which function would be most severely impaired?
items.explanation: WHITE BLOOD CELLS (leucocytes) are responsible for IMMUNE DEFENCE - they engulf bacteria (phagocytosis), produce antibodies, and fight infections. Very low WBC count (leucopenia) severely compromises immunity, leaving the person vulnerable to infections. Oxygen transport depends on RBCs (haemoglobin). Blood pressure is regulated by heart and blood vessels. Blood clotting depends on platelets and clotting factors.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Plants have two separate transport systems: XYLEM for transporting water and minerals from roots upward, and PHLOEM for transporting food (photosynthetic products) from leaves to all parts of the plant (upward and downward).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: XYLEM: Conducts water and dissolved minerals from roots to all parts. One-way (upward) transport. Composed of VESSELS and TRACHEIDS (dead cells). Driving forces: Root pressure + Transpiration pull.
ROOT PRESSURE: Root cells absorb ions actively, creating osmotic gradient; water enters roots from soil by osmosis; creates upward push.
TRANSPIRATION PULL: Evaporation of water from leaf cells through stomata (transpiration) creates suction that pulls water up through xylem.

PHLOEM: Transports food (sucrose, amino acids) from LEAVES (where produced by photosynthesis) to all parts including roots, growing tips, fruits, seeds. Bidirectional (up and down). Composed of living SIEVE TUBE CELLS + COMPANION CELLS. Requires ENERGY (ATP) for loading sucrose into phloem (ACTIVE TRANSPORT).
TRANSLOCATION: The process of moving photosynthetic products through phloem. Driven by osmotic pressure differences.
TRANSPIRATION: Loss of water as vapour from leaves (mainly through stomata). Benefits: (a) Drives water transport in xylem. (b) Cools the plant. (c) Enables upward movement of minerals.
Plants have LOW ENERGY NEEDS (non-motile, many dead cells in tissues); therefore transport systems can be slower.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 5.8 (p.53):
sections.aim: To demonstrate that transpiration is the driving force for water movement in xylem.
sections.materials: Two small pots of same size with soil; one pot with a plant, one with a stick (same height); plastic sheets to cover soil; sunlight.
procedure: - Cover soil in both pots with plastic sheet (to prevent soil evaporation).
- Place both in sunlight for 30 minutes.
- Observe difference (or observe water condensation on plastic covers).
sections.observation: Pot with plant shows moisture condensation on the plastic sheet (water vapour from transpiration). Pot with stick shows little or no moisture.
sections.conclusion:
The plant loses water through transpiration from its leaves. Transpiration drives the upward movement of water in the xylem, as water lost from leaves is continuously replaced by water pulled up from roots.

items.question: What is transpiration? What is its importance?
items.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant (mainly through stomata on leaves and stems). Importance: (1) It is the main driving force for upward movement of water and minerals through xylem (creates transpiration pull). (2) It helps in cooling the plant. (3) It aids in the upward transport of minerals dissolved in water.

items.question: Explain the role of root pressure and transpiration pull in water transport in plants.
items.answer:
Water transport through xylem is driven by two forces:
(i) ROOT PRESSURE: Root cells actively absorb mineral ions from soil using energy. This creates a HIGH concentration of solutes in root cells compared to soil water. Water therefore enters root cells by OSMOSIS from the soil. This osmotic entry of water creates a push (ROOT PRESSURE) that moves water into xylem and begins to push it upward. However, root pressure alone is insufficient for tall trees.
(ii) TRANSPIRATION PULL (main force): Water evaporates from mesophyll cells of leaves through stomata. This evaporation lowers the water content of leaf cells, creating a suction. Water is pulled from xylem vessels in the leaf veins to replace lost water. This pull is transmitted all the way down through the continuous xylem column to the roots, drawing water upward from the soil. This TRANSPIRATION PULL is the primary driving force in tall plants.

items.question: Describe translocation in plants. How does food move through the phloem?
items.answer:
TRANSLOCATION is the transport of photosynthetic products (primarily sucrose, along with amino acids) from leaves (SOURCE) to all other parts of the plant (SINKS: roots, stems, growing buds, fruits, seeds) through the PHLOEM.
MECHANISM:
(i) LOADING: Sucrose produced in leaf mesophyll cells is ACTIVELY LOADED into the sieve tubes of phloem at the source (leaves) using ATP energy. This increases the concentration of solutes (sucrose) in phloem sieve tubes.
(ii) WATER ENTRY: High solute concentration in phloem causes water to move into phloem from adjacent xylem by OSMOSIS. This increases PRESSURE (turgor pressure) in phloem at the source end.
(iii) PRESSURE-DRIVEN FLOW: The increased pressure at the source pushes phloem contents (sucrose solution) toward SINKS (areas of lower solute concentration - roots, fruits, growing buds) where sucrose is used up or stored. Pressure at sink end is lower.
(iv) UNLOADING: At the sink, sucrose is unloaded from phloem into sink cells (used for growth, respiration, storage). Water leaves phloem back to xylem.
DIRECTION: Translocation in phloem is BIDIRECTIONAL (can move upward and downward) unlike xylem which is only upward. For example, in spring, stored sugars in roots are transported upward to growing buds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which tissue in plants is responsible for transporting water and minerals from roots?
items.explanation: XYLEM is the vascular tissue responsible for upward transport of water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves and other parts. PHLOEM transports food. Cambium is a meristematic tissue that produces xylem and phloem. Epidermis is the outer covering layer.

items.question: The transport of food through phloem is called:
items.explanation: TRANSLOCATION is the term for the movement of soluble food products (sucrose, amino acids) through phloem tissue from leaves to other plant parts. Transpiration is water loss from leaves. Respiration is energy release from food. Absorption is uptake of water/minerals by roots.

items.question: Why does phloem transport require energy (ATP) while xylem transport does not?

options.B: Because sucrose must be ACTIVELY LOADED into phloem sieve tubes against the concentration gradient, requiring ATP
options.C: Because phloem must move faster than xylem
options.D: Because ATP keeps phloem cells alive

items.explanation: Sucrose (at high concentration in leaves) must be loaded INTO phloem sieve tubes AGAINST a concentration gradient - this requires ACTIVE TRANSPORT using ATP energy. In contrast, xylem transport is driven by physical forces (root pressure - osmosis, and transpiration pull - suction) - passive processes that do not require ATP. Xylem cells are actually dead and have no metabolic activity.

items.question: In the spring season, stored sugars in the roots of a tree move upward to the growing buds. What does this demonstrate about phloem transport?

options.B: Phloem transport is bidirectional (can move both up and down)
options.C: Xylem carries the sugars upward in spring

items.explanation: The movement of stored sugars from ROOTS upward to growing BUDS demonstrates that phloem transport is BIDIRECTIONAL. Normally food moves from leaves (where made) downward to roots. But when needed, stored food in roots is transported upward to growing parts. This is in contrast to xylem, which always transports water only upward.

items.question: If all the stomata of a plant are permanently closed (e.g., coated with wax), what would be the most significant effect on plant transport?

options.B: Xylem water transport would severely slow down as transpiration pull is eliminated

items.explanation: Stomata are the main exit points for water vapour (transpiration). TRANSPIRATION PULL is the primary driving force for water movement through xylem in tall plants. If stomata are blocked, transpiration stops, eliminating transpiration pull. Water movement through xylem would be severely reduced (only weak root pressure remains). This would also block CO2 entry (reducing photosynthesis - option D is wrong). Phloem transport (option A) uses active loading, not transpiration. Root pressure (option C) is not affected by stomata closure.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Excretion is the biological process by which harmful metabolic waste products generated during cellular activities are removed from the body of an organism.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Metabolic activities (respiration, protein metabolism) produce waste: CO2, water, nitrogenous compounds (urea, uric acid), excess salts.
If wastes accumulate, they become toxic and can kill cells or the organism.
UNICELLULAR ORGANISMS: Remove waste by simple diffusion over the body surface.
MULTICELLULAR ORGANISMS: Use specialised excretory organs.
In HUMAN BEINGS: Kidneys (filter blood, produce urine - nitrogenous waste); Lungs (excrete CO2 and water vapour); Skin (sweating - some urea and salts).
In PLANTS: Different strategies (no specialised excretory organs).
CO2 (from respiration) and O2 (from photosynthesis) removed by diffusion through stomata.
Excess water removed by transpiration.
Solid wastes stored in CELL VACUOLES, old bark, or in RESINS and GUMS.
Some waste excreted into soil around roots.
Waste products may be stored in falling leaves.
EXCRETION (In-text Questions - p.66):
Q: Describe the structure and functioning of nephrons.
A: (See Sub-topic 5.5.1 Q&A below)
Q: What are the methods used by plants to get rid of excretory products?
A: (See Sub-topic 5.5.2)
Q: How is the amount of urine produced regulated?

A: The amount of urine produced depends on: (1) How much excess water is in the body. (2) How much dissolved waste needs to be excreted. If excess water is available, more dilute and more urine is produced. If water is scarce, the kidney reabsorbs more water from the tubule and produces concentrated, less urine.

items.question: What is excretion? Why is it necessary?
items.answer: Excretion is the process by which metabolic waste products (CO2, urea, uric acid, excess salts) produced during cellular activities are removed from the body. It is necessary because: (1) These waste products are toxic and if they accumulate they can damage cells and tissues. (2) Maintaining proper chemical balance (homeostasis) of body fluids requires removal of excess substances.

items.question: Name the organs involved in excretion in human beings and the substances excreted by each.
items.answer: (1) KIDNEYS: Filter blood and remove nitrogenous wastes (primarily UREA, also uric acid, excess salts, water) in the form of URINE. (2) LUNGS: Excrete CARBON DIOXIDE and WATER VAPOUR during exhalation. (3) SKIN: Sweat glands excrete small amounts of UREA, LACTIC ACID, and SALTS in sweat.

items.question: Describe the structure of the human excretory system.
items.answer:
The human excretory system consists of:
(i) A pair of KIDNEYS: Bean-shaped organs located in the abdomen on either side of the backbone. Each kidney contains millions of filtration units called NEPHRONS. They filter blood to produce urine.
(ii) A pair of URETERS: Tubes connecting each kidney to the urinary bladder; carry urine from kidneys to the bladder.
(iii) URINARY BLADDER: A muscular sac that stores urine until it is ready to be passed out. It is under NERVOUS CONTROL.
(iv) URETHRA: A tube through which urine is released from the bladder to the outside of the body. The exit is controlled by the urethral sphincter.

items.question: Describe the structure and functioning of a nephron.
items.answer:
NEPHRON is the basic structural and functional unit of the kidney. Each kidney has millions of nephrons.
STRUCTURE:
(i) BOWMAN'S CAPSULE: Cup-shaped structure at one end of the nephron. Inside it is a tuft of capillaries called the GLOMERULUS (a branch of the renal artery).
(ii) TUBULAR PART: A long coiled tube leading from Bowman's capsule; surrounded by a network of capillaries (branch of renal vein).
(iii) COLLECTING DUCT: The tube leads into a collecting duct that carries urine to the ureter.
FUNCTIONING:
(i) FILTRATION: Blood enters the glomerulus under high pressure. Small molecules (water, glucose, amino acids, urea, salts) are forced from the capillaries into the Bowman's capsule as the INITIAL FILTRATE. Large molecules (proteins, blood cells) remain in blood.
(ii) REABSORPTION: As the initial filtrate passes through the tubular part, useful substances (glucose, amino acids, most water, some salts) are SELECTIVELY REABSORBED back into the surrounding capillaries. The amount of water reabsorbed depends on body needs.
(iii) URINE FORMATION: What remains in the tubule after reabsorption (concentrated urea, excess salts, some water) forms URINE. This urine collects in collecting duct --> ureter --> bladder --> urethra --> outside.

items.question: How do plants excrete their waste products? Compare plant excretion with animal excretion.
items.answer:
PLANT EXCRETION:
Plants do not have specialised excretory organs but use various strategies:
(i) O2 (waste from photosynthesis): Released into air by DIFFUSION through stomata.
(ii) CO2 and water vapour (waste from respiration): Released through stomata.
(iii) Excess water: Removed by TRANSPIRATION through stomata.
(iv) Solid metabolic wastes: Stored in CELLULAR VACUOLES in leaves, bark, and stem cells.
(v) Resins, gums, tannins, oils: Stored in old xylem wood (heartwood).
(vi) Waste in leaves: Some plants store waste products in leaves that fall off annually, removing wastes.
(vii) Soil excretion: Some waste substances are excreted into soil around roots.

COMPARISON:
Feature - Animal Excretion - Plant Excretion
Specialised organs - Yes (kidneys, lungs) - No
Main nitrogenous waste - Urea (humans) - Very little (mainly CO2)
Energy used - Yes (active processes) - Mostly passive
Products - Urine, CO2, sweat - CO2, O2, water, stored resins/gums
Plants generate less nitrogenous waste as they do not move, do not maintain body temperature, and have lower metabolic rates.

items.question: Describe in detail how the kidney filters blood and regulates the amount of urine produced.
items.answer:
KIDNEY STRUCTURE:
Each kidney contains about 1 million NEPHRONS arranged in the cortex and medulla. Blood is supplied to kidneys via RENAL ARTERY (branch of aorta); filtered blood returns via RENAL VEIN.

URINE FORMATION (3 steps):
(i) ULTRAFILTRATION (Glomerulus + Bowman's Capsule):
- Blood enters the GLOMERULUS (tuft of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule) under HIGH PRESSURE.
- Due to this pressure, water, glucose, amino acids, urea, salts, uric acid are forced through the thin capillary walls into BOWMAN'S CAPSULE as INITIAL FILTRATE (~180 L/day in humans!).
- Large molecules (proteins, blood cells) cannot pass through; remain in blood.

(ii) SELECTIVE REABSORPTION (Tubule):
- As initial filtrate flows through the long tubular part, the surrounding capillaries reabsorb useful substances:
- ALL glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed (normally none in urine).
- Large amounts of WATER are reabsorbed.
- Some salts are reabsorbed.
- This selective reabsorption ensures essential nutrients are not lost.

(iii) CONCENTRATION AND URINE FORMATION:
- What remains: concentrated UREA + excess salts + some water = URINE (~1-2 L/day excreted).
- Urine flows: tubule --> collecting duct --> ureter --> URINARY BLADDER (stored) --> URETHRA --> excreted.

REGULATION OF URINE VOLUME:
- If the body has EXCESS WATER: Less water is reabsorbed by tubules --> MORE, DILUTE URINE produced.
- If the body is DEHYDRATED: More water is reabsorbed by tubules (under hormonal control - ADH/antidiuretic hormone) --> LESS, CONCENTRATED URINE produced.
- UREA CONCENTRATION: More waste to excrete = more urine produced.
- URINARY BLADDER under NERVOUS CONTROL: Pressure from filling bladder sends signals to the brain; urination is controlled voluntarily by the urethral sphincter.

ARTIFICIAL KIDNEY (HEMODIALYSIS): When kidneys fail, an artificial kidney machine performs dialysis - blood is passed through tubes with a selectively permeable membrane surrounded by dialysing fluid (same composition as blood plasma but without wastes). Wastes diffuse out; purified blood is returned. The initial filtrate in healthy kidneys is ~180 L/day, but only 1-2 L of urine is excreted because the remaining 178+ L is reabsorbed by tubules.

items.question: The functional unit of the kidney is called:
items.explanation: The NEPHRON is the basic structural and functional unit of the kidney - each kidney has about one million nephrons. The GLOMERULUS is part of the nephron (the capillary tuft inside Bowman's capsule). Alveolus is the air sac in lungs. Villus is the projection in small intestine.

items.question: What is the main nitrogenous waste product excreted by human kidneys?
items.explanation: The primary nitrogenous waste in humans is UREA, formed in the liver from the breakdown of excess amino acids. Urea is filtered by the kidneys and excreted in urine. CO2 is excreted by the lungs. Ammonia is toxic and is converted to urea. Uric acid is excreted in smaller amounts (mainly from nucleic acid breakdown).

items.question: Urine formed in the kidneys is carried to the urinary bladder by:
items.explanation: URETERS are the tubes (one from each kidney) that carry urine from the kidneys to the URINARY BLADDER for storage. The URETHRA carries urine from the bladder to the outside. The renal artery and vein carry blood (not urine) to and from the kidney.

items.question: In the process of urine formation, which substances are selectively reabsorbed from the tubular filtrate back into the blood?

options.B: Glucose, amino acids, and most water

items.explanation: During SELECTIVE REABSORPTION in kidney tubules, useful substances - glucose (all of it), amino acids (all of it), and most water - are reabsorbed back into the surrounding capillaries. Urea and excess salts are NOT reabsorbed (or only partially) as they are waste products to be excreted. Proteins and blood cells are too large to be filtered in the first place. CO2 is not handled by the kidney.

items.question: Why do plants not need specialised excretory organs unlike animals?

options.A: Plants do not produce any waste
options.B: Plants produce very little nitrogenous waste and can store/reuse/remove gaseous waste by diffusion; their low metabolic rate makes complex excretion unnecessary
options.C: Plants excrete waste through their flowers
options.D: Plants absorb waste products from the soil

items.explanation: Plants produce far less nitrogenous waste than animals because they do not digest proteins in large quantities and are non-motile (lower metabolic rate). Their main gaseous wastes (CO2 and O2) are removed by diffusion through stomata. Solid wastes are stored in vacuoles, bark, or shed leaves. The simplicity of their waste management means no specialised organ is needed. Option A is incorrect (plants DO produce waste).

items.question: A healthy person's urine normally does NOT contain:
items.explanation: Normally, all GLUCOSE filtered from blood is COMPLETELY REABSORBED by kidney tubules back into blood. Therefore, healthy urine does NOT contain glucose. Presence of glucose in urine (glucosuria) is a sign of diabetes mellitus. Urea (main waste), water, and excess salts are all normal components of urine.

items.question: In haemodialysis (artificial kidney), the patient's blood is passed through tubes with a selectively permeable membrane surrounded by dialysing fluid. What is the composition of this dialysing fluid?

options.A: Pure distilled water to maximise waste removal
options.B: Same composition as blood plasma but WITHOUT nitrogenous wastes (so wastes diffuse out by concentration gradient)
options.C: Concentrated urea solution to pull wastes from blood

items.explanation: Dialysing fluid has the SAME OSMOTIC COMPOSITION as normal blood plasma (normal concentrations of glucose, salts, etc.) but is DEVOID of nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid). This creates a CONCENTRATION GRADIENT for wastes to diffuse FROM blood INTO dialysing fluid. If pure water were used, all useful solutes (glucose, salts) would also diffuse out. This clever design removes only waste products while retaining essential blood components.

items.question: The initial filtrate volume in kidneys is about 180 L per day, but only about 1-2 L of urine is produced. What happens to the remaining ~178 L of water?

options.A: It is stored in the urinary bladder and released slowly
options.B: It is selectively reabsorbed from the kidney tubules back into the blood capillaries
options.D: It is excreted through the lungs

items.explanation: Of the ~180 L of initial filtrate formed in Bowman's capsules daily, approximately 178+ L of water is SELECTIVELY REABSORBED from the kidney tubules back into the surrounding capillaries. This reabsorption recovers all glucose, amino acids, and most water, making the process energy-intensive but essential for fluid conservation. Only ~1-2 L of concentrated waste (urine) is excreted. The reabsorbed water returns to circulation via the renal vein.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Excretion in human beings is primarily carried out by the KIDNEYS which filter blood to remove nitrogenous waste (urea) as URINE. Other organs (lungs for CO2, skin for sweat) also contribute to excretion.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: EXCRETORY SYSTEM: Kidneys (pair) + Ureters (pair) + Urinary Bladder + Urethra.
KIDNEYS: Located in abdomen on either side of the backbone.
Each kidney has millions of NEPHRONS.
Blood enters via RENAL ARTERY; filtered blood exits via RENAL VEIN.
NEPHRON (basic filtration unit):
BOWMAN'S CAPSULE: Cup-shaped; contains GLOMERULUS (capillary tuft from renal artery).
TUBULAR PART: Long coiled tube surrounded by capillaries.
COLLECTING DUCT: Final tube leading to ureter.
URINE FORMATION (3 stages):
FILTRATION: Small molecules forced into Bowman's capsule (initial filtrate ~180 L/day).
REABSORPTION: Glucose, amino acids, most water reabsorbed by tubules.
CONCENTRATION: Urea, excess salts, small water amount remain as urine (~1-2 L/day).
URINARY BLADDER: Muscular sac; stores urine; under NERVOUS CONTROL.
URETHRA: Carries urine out; controlled by urethral sphincter.
ARTIFICIAL KIDNEY (HEMODIALYSIS): Used when kidneys fail; uses selectively permeable membrane and dialysing fluid to filter blood externally.
MORE TO KNOW (p.65):
ARTIFICIAL KIDNEY (HEMODIALYSIS):
Kidneys are vital. Infections, injury, or restricted blood flow can reduce kidney activity, causing accumulation of poisonous wastes.
Artificial kidney contains tubes with semi-permeable lining in a tank with dialysing fluid.
Dialysing fluid: same osmotic composition as blood plasma but NO nitrogenous wastes.
Patient's blood from artery passes through semi-permeable tubes; wastes diffuse out by concentration gradient into dialysing fluid; purified blood is pumped back into vein.
Normal initial filtrate: ~180 L/day; actual urine: ~1-2 L/day (rest is reabsorbed).

items.question: What is haemodialysis (artificial kidney)? When is it needed?
items.answer: Haemodialysis is the process of filtering blood using an artificial kidney machine when the patient's own kidneys are failing. It is needed when kidney failure causes accumulation of toxic nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid) in the blood. In haemodialysis, blood is passed through tubes with a semi-permeable membrane surrounded by dialysing fluid; wastes diffuse out into the fluid; purified blood is returned to the patient.

items.question: Describe the filtration and reabsorption that occurs in a nephron.
items.answer:
FILTRATION (Glomerulus + Bowman's Capsule):
- Blood enters the GLOMERULUS (capillary tuft) under HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE.
- Small molecules (water, glucose, amino acids, urea, salts) are FILTERED through the thin capillary walls into the surrounding BOWMAN'S CAPSULE as INITIAL FILTRATE.
- Large molecules (proteins, blood cells) remain in blood.
REABSORPTION (Tubular Part):
- As filtrate flows through the tubular part, surrounding blood capillaries SELECTIVELY REABSORB:
* ALL glucose (100%)
* ALL amino acids (100%)
* Most water (about 99%)
* Some salts (depending on body needs)
- Energy (ATP) is used for active reabsorption of glucose and amino acids.
- What remains: concentrated urea, excess salts, and a small amount of water = URINE.

items.question: How is the amount of urine produced regulated by the body?
items.answer:
The amount of urine produced is regulated by SELECTIVE REABSORPTION of water in the kidney tubules:

(i) WHEN BODY HAS EXCESS WATER:
- Less water is reabsorbed from the tubules.
- More water passes into collecting duct and leaves as urine.
- Result: LARGE AMOUNT of DILUTE urine.

(ii) WHEN BODY IS DEHYDRATED:
- More water is reabsorbed from tubules back into blood (under hormonal control - ADH: Antidiuretic Hormone from pituitary gland increases water reabsorption).
- Very little water passes into collecting duct.
- Result: SMALL AMOUNT of CONCENTRATED urine.

(iii) WASTE LEVELS:
- If more nitrogenous waste (urea) needs to be excreted, urine volume increases.

(iv) URINATION CONTROL:
- Urine is stored in the URINARY BLADDER (under nervous control).
- When the bladder is full, stretch receptors signal the brain; urination is controlled voluntarily through the URETHRAL SPHINCTER.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The cup-shaped structure at the beginning of a nephron that collects filtered material from the glomerulus is:
items.explanation: BOWMAN'S CAPSULE is the cup-shaped beginning of the nephron that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the initial filtrate. The ureter carries urine from kidney to bladder. The collecting duct collects urine from many nephrons. The urethra carries urine out of the body.

items.question: Urine is stored in the body in the:
items.explanation: Urine formed in the kidneys passes through URETERS and is stored in the URINARY BLADDER until excreted through the URETHRA. The kidney is where urine is made, not stored. The ureter is a transport tube, not a storage organ. The urethra is the exit passage.

items.question: What substance in the dialysing fluid of an artificial kidney ensures that glucose and useful salts are NOT lost from the patient's blood during dialysis?

options.A: Urea at the same concentration as blood
options.B: Glucose and salts at the SAME concentrations as in normal blood plasma

items.explanation: The dialysing fluid contains glucose and salts at the SAME concentrations as in normal blood plasma. Because there is no concentration gradient for glucose or normal salts between blood and dialysing fluid, they do NOT diffuse out of the blood. Only UREA (absent from dialysing fluid but present in blood) diffuses out down its concentration gradient. This clever design ensures only waste products are removed.

items.question: If the tubular part of a nephron loses its ability to reabsorb glucose, what would happen?

options.B: Glucose would appear in the urine (glucosuria)

items.explanation: Normally, ALL glucose filtered in Bowman's capsule is REABSORBED by the tubular part back into blood. If reabsorption fails, glucose remains in the tubular fluid and is excreted in urine - a condition called GLUCOSURIA. This also occurs in DIABETES MELLITUS when blood glucose is so high that the tubule cannot reabsorb all of it. Urea excretion and Bowman's filtration are independent of glucose reabsorption.

items.question: A person lives in a very hot, dry desert and sweats heavily. How would the body adjust kidney function to compensate?

options.A: Increase urine production to remove excess salts
options.B: Decrease water reabsorption to maintain hydration
options.C: Increase water reabsorption in kidney tubules and produce concentrated urine to conserve water

items.explanation: In hot, dry conditions with heavy sweating, the body LOSES WATER. To prevent dehydration, the kidneys INCREASE water reabsorption from tubules (controlled by ADH - antidiuretic hormone, released when blood becomes concentrated). This produces SMALL amounts of HIGHLY CONCENTRATED urine, conserving water. Decreasing reabsorption (option B) would worsen dehydration. The body cannot stop urine production entirely as waste must still be excreted.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Plants excrete waste products produced during photosynthesis and respiration using simple diffusion through stomata and by storing solid wastes in various plant structures. They lack specialised excretory organs.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Plants produce less waste than animals because: (1) They are non-motile (low energy demands). (2) Many tissues consist of dead cells. (3) They produce very little nitrogenous waste (do not digest proteins extensively).
GASEOUS WASTES:
OXYGEN (from photosynthesis): Released through stomata by diffusion.
CARBON DIOXIDE (from respiration): Released through stomata (but used for photosynthesis during day).
Excess water: Released as vapour through stomata (transpiration).
SOLID WASTES:
Stored in CELLULAR VACUOLES as waste products.
Stored as RESINS and GUMS in old xylem wood (heartwood).
Stored in BARK cells (shed periodically).
Some waste excreted into SOIL around roots.
Stored in LEAVES that fall off (deciduous trees shed waste with autumn leaves).
Plants can use certain waste products as raw materials: CO2 (respiration waste) is reused for photosynthesis during the day.
Oxygen (photosynthesis waste) is used for respiration.

items.question: How do plants excrete gaseous waste products?
items.answer:
Plants excrete gaseous waste products primarily by DIFFUSION through STOMATA (pores on leaf and stem surfaces):
(1) OXYGEN produced during photosynthesis diffuses out through stomata when not needed for respiration.
(2) CARBON DIOXIDE produced during respiration diffuses out through stomata (or is reused for photosynthesis during daytime).
(3) Excess water vapour is released through stomata as TRANSPIRATION.
Intercellular air spaces inside leaves ensure all cells are in contact with air for efficient diffusion.

items.question: Compare the methods by which plants and animals excrete solid/non-gaseous waste.
items.answer:
ANIMALS (e.g., human beings):
- Main solid/non-gaseous waste: UREA (nitrogenous), excess salts.
- Excreted by KIDNEYS as URINE (aqueous solution).
- Active process requiring energy and specialised organs.
- Waste is immediately removed from the body.

PLANTS:
- Generate very little nitrogenous waste (not much protein digestion).
- Non-gaseous wastes are STORED in the plant body, not immediately removed:
(1) Stored in CELLULAR VACUOLES (leaf cells, bark cells).
(2) Stored as RESINS and GUMS in dead xylem (heartwood).
(3) Removed with falling LEAVES in deciduous plants.
(4) Some excreted into SOIL around roots.
- Passive process; no specialised excretory organs needed.

KEY DIFFERENCE: Animals excrete waste immediately and efficiently. Plants store or passively remove waste products.

items.question: Why do plants not need specialised excretory organs? Explain in detail.
items.answer:
Plants do not need specialised excretory organs for the following reasons:
(i) LOW NITROGENOUS WASTE: Animals produce large amounts of nitrogenous waste (urea) from protein digestion and metabolism. Plants produce very little nitrogenous waste because they do not digest proteins in large quantities; their nitrogen (from soil nitrates) is mostly incorporated into structural molecules and is not frequently broken down.
(ii) WASTE REUSE: Plants can reuse their "waste" products: CO2 (respiratory waste) is used as raw material for photosynthesis; O2 (photosynthetic waste) is used for respiration. This recycling reduces the burden of excretion.
(iii) PASSIVE DIFFUSION SUFFICIENT FOR GASES: Gaseous wastes (CO2, O2, water vapour) are small molecules that can be removed by simple DIFFUSION through stomata and large intercellular air spaces in leaves. No active transport or specialised organ needed.
(iv) LOW METABOLIC RATE: Plants are non-motile and many of their tissues consist of dead cells. Their overall metabolic rate and waste production is lower than that of animals.
(v) STORAGE CAPACITY: Plants can STORE solid waste products in vacuoles, bark, leaves, gums, and resins without harm. Some of these (like resins) may even serve protective functions. When leaves fall, stored waste is removed. This strategy means excretion does not need to be continuous or immediate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which gas produced as a waste product during photosynthesis is beneficial as a raw material for respiration?
items.explanation: OXYGEN is produced as a waste/by-product of photosynthesis (from splitting of water molecules). This same oxygen is used as the raw material for AEROBIC RESPIRATION in the plant itself (and in all aerobic organisms). CO2 is the waste of respiration and raw material of photosynthesis. Nitrogen and water vapour are not waste products of photosynthesis.

items.question: Plants store solid waste products in:

options.B: Cellular vacuoles, bark, and as resins/gums in old wood

items.explanation: Plants store solid waste in CELLULAR VACUOLES (in leaf and bark cells), in old BARK (which is shed), and as RESINS and GUMS in the dead xylem wood (heartwood). Some waste is also stored in leaves that fall off. Xylem sap carries water and minerals. Phloem carries food. Root cells do not primarily store waste.

items.question: During the day, a plant simultaneously produces CO2 (respiration waste) and uses CO2 (for photosynthesis). What happens to the NET CO2 exchange?

options.A: CO2 is always released since respiration is continuous
options.B: During active photosynthesis, the CO2 produced by respiration is completely consumed, so net CO2 release = zero; instead O2 is the main output
options.D: The plant stops respiration during the day

items.explanation: During active photosynthesis in bright light, the rate of CO2 consumption (for photosynthesis) exceeds CO2 production (from respiration). Respiration's CO2 is fully consumed, and net CO2 exchange is essentially zero or slightly inward. Instead, O2 is the main gas released. At NIGHT (no photosynthesis), CO2 from respiration is released and O2 is consumed - the reverse pattern. This is the basis of the textbook statement: "During the day, CO2 generated during respiration is used up for photosynthesis, hence there is no net CO2 release."

items.question: When leaves fall in autumn (deciduous trees), what excretory function does this serve?

options.A: It allows more sunlight to reach soil
options.B: Leaves contain accumulated waste products; shedding removes these wastes from the plant

items.explanation: Falling leaves serve BOTH excretory AND water conservation functions: (B) Plants store non-gaseous waste products in leaf vacuoles; shedding leaves removes these accumulated wastes from the plant body - an excretory mechanism. (C) Deciduous trees also shed leaves to prevent water loss through transpiration during dry/cold seasons when water is scarce. Both reasons are valid and stated in the textbook.

items.question: A student argues that since plants can reuse both CO2 and O2, they do not truly excrete anything. Is this correct?

options.A: Yes, since all plant waste products are recycled
options.B: No, because plants cannot always use all the CO2 and O2 produced; excess gases are released through stomata; solid wastes in bark, vacuoles, and resins are also excreted or stored and shed
options.C: Yes, plants only need excretion at night
options.D: No, because plants excrete only nitrogen compounds like animals

items.explanation: While plants DO reuse CO2 (from respiration) and O2 (from photosynthesis), this is not always complete: At night, all CO2 from respiration is released (no photosynthesis to consume it). Excess O2 from photosynthesis is released when it exceeds respiratory needs. Additionally, solid waste products (resins, gums, tannins) accumulate in bark and vacuoles and cannot be reused - they are eventually removed by bark shedding or leaf fall. Therefore, plants DO excrete, just using simpler, passive mechanisms. Option D is wrong - plants produce very little nitrogenous waste.

sections.label: EXERCISE 5 - Full Chapter Exercises:

items.question: The kidneys in human beings are a part of the system for
items.answer:
(a) nutrition  (b) respiration  (c) excretion  (d) transportation
ANSWER: (c) excretion
EXPLANATION: Kidneys are part of the excretory system; they filter blood to remove urea and other nitrogenous wastes as urine.

items.question: The xylem in plants are responsible for
items.answer:
(a) transport of water  (b) transport of food  (c) transport of amino acids  (d) transport of oxygen
ANSWER: (a) transport of water
EXPLANATION: XYLEM carries water and dissolved minerals from roots upward. PHLOEM carries food.

items.question: The autotrophic mode of nutrition requires
items.answer:
(a) carbon dioxide and water  (b) chlorophyll  (c) sunlight  (d) all of the above
ANSWER: (d) all of the above
EXPLANATION: Autotrophic nutrition (photosynthesis) requires CO2, water, chlorophyll, and sunlight - all of these together.

items.question: The breakdown of pyruvate to give carbon dioxide, water and energy takes place in
items.answer:
(a) cytoplasm  (b) mitochondria  (c) chloroplast  (d) nucleus
ANSWER: (b) mitochondria
EXPLANATION: Aerobic breakdown of pyruvate (the 3-carbon molecule from glycolysis) occurs in the MITOCHONDRIA in the presence of oxygen.

items.question: How are fats digested in our bodies? Where does this process take place?
items.answer:
ANSWER: Fats are digested in the SMALL INTESTINE.
STEP 1: Bile juice (from liver, stored in gall bladder) is released into the small intestine. Bile EMULSIFIES fats - it breaks large fat globules into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.
STEP 2: PANCREATIC LIPASE (from pancreas) acts on the emulsified fat droplets.
STEP 3: Intestinal glands also secrete LIPASE which completes fat digestion.
PRODUCTS: Fatty acids and glycerol (final absorbable products of fat digestion).
ABSORPTION: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed through villi into the lymphatic capillaries (lacteals) in the villi, then carried to blood circulation.

items.question: What is the role of saliva in the digestion of food?
items.answer:
ANSWER: Saliva plays two important roles:
(1) MECHANICAL: Saliva is secreted by salivary glands and WETS the food, making it smooth and easy to swallow. It lubricates the food bolus for easy movement through the oesophagus.
(2) CHEMICAL: Saliva contains the enzyme SALIVARY AMYLASE (ptyalin) which begins the chemical digestion of STARCH - it breaks starch (complex carbohydrate) into MALTOSE (a simpler sugar). This is the first step of chemical digestion in the body.

items.question: What are the necessary conditions for autotrophic nutrition and what are its by-products?
items.answer:
ANSWER: NECESSARY CONDITIONS for autotrophic nutrition (photosynthesis):
(1) CARBON DIOXIDE: Absorbed from air through stomata.
(2) WATER: Absorbed from soil through roots.
(3) CHLOROPHYLL: The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy.
(4) SUNLIGHT: The energy source that powers photosynthesis.
BY-PRODUCTS of autotrophic nutrition:
(1) OXYGEN: Released as a by-product when water molecules are split during photosynthesis. (Beneficial - used for respiration by all aerobic organisms.)
(2) WATER: Also released during photosynthesis as a by-product.
NOTE: Glucose (the primary product) is not a by-product; it is the main useful product.

items.question: What are the differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration? Name some organisms that use anaerobic mode of respiration.
items.answer:
ANSWER:
AEROBIC RESPIRATION:
- Requires OXYGEN.
- Pyruvate is broken down in MITOCHONDRIA.
- Products: CO2 + H2O + Large amount of energy.
- ENERGY YIELD: High (~38 ATP).
- Example: Humans, most animals and plants.

ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION:
- Does NOT require oxygen.
- Occurs in CYTOPLASM only.
- Products: In yeast: Ethanol + CO2 + Small energy. In muscle cells: Lactic acid + Small energy.
- ENERGY YIELD: Low (~2 ATP).
- Example: Yeast, some bacteria, muscle cells (during sudden strenuous activity).

- YEAST (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) - fermentation
- LACTOBACILLUS - produces lactic acid in milk (yogurt making)
- Some bacteria in swamps and intestines
- Human muscle cells (temporarily during intense exercise)

items.question: How are the alveoli designed to maximise the exchange of gases?
items.answer:
ANSWER: Alveoli are designed to maximise gas exchange in the following ways:
(1) LARGE NUMBER: Millions of alveoli in each lung, providing a HUGE TOTAL SURFACE AREA (~80 m2 if spread out - much larger than body surface area).
(2) THIN WALLS: Alveolar walls are only ONE CELL THICK - very thin and moist, reducing the distance for diffusion of gases.
(3) RICH BLOOD SUPPLY: Each alveolus is surrounded by a dense network of BLOOD CAPILLARIES, ensuring that gas exchange occurs between alveolar air and blood continuously and efficiently.
(4) BALLOON-LIKE STRUCTURE: Alveoli are balloon-shaped, maximising volume for their surface area.
(5) RESIDUAL VOLUME: Lungs always retain some air (residual volume), ensuring there is always sufficient time for oxygen to be absorbed and CO2 to be released - continuous gas exchange.

items.question: What would be the consequences of a deficiency of haemoglobin in our bodies?
items.answer:
ANSWER: Haemoglobin deficiency (ANAEMIA) would have the following consequences:
(1) REDUCED OXYGEN TRANSPORT: Less haemoglobin means less oxygen can be carried from lungs to tissues.
(2) CELLULAR ENERGY DEFICIT: Reduced oxygen supply impairs aerobic respiration in cells, reducing ATP production. This leads to FATIGUE, WEAKNESS, and reduced physical performance.
(3) BREATHLESSNESS: The body tries to compensate by increasing breathing rate and heart rate.
(4) PALE SKIN: Since haemoglobin gives blood its red colour, deficiency leads to pale skin and mucous membranes.
(5) IMPAIRED ORGAN FUNCTION: In severe cases, reduced oxygen supply can affect brain function (dizziness, difficulty concentrating) and heart function (strain on heart as it pumps faster to compensate).
(6) MUSCLE CRAMPS: Cells may resort to anaerobic respiration more frequently, building up lactic acid.

items.question: Describe double circulation of blood in human beings. Why is it necessary?
items.answer:
ANSWER: DOUBLE CIRCULATION means blood passes through the heart TWICE in one complete circuit.
CIRCUIT 1 - PULMONARY CIRCULATION:
- Deoxygenated blood: Right Atrium --> Right Ventricle --> Pulmonary Arteries --> LUNGS.
- In lungs: CO2 released, O2 absorbed (oxygenation).
- Oxygenated blood: Lungs --> Pulmonary Veins --> Left Atrium.
CIRCUIT 2 - SYSTEMIC CIRCULATION:
- Oxygenated blood: Left Atrium --> Left Ventricle --> AORTA --> ALL BODY ORGANS.
- In tissues: O2 and nutrients delivered; CO2 and waste collected.
- Deoxygenated blood: All organs --> VENA CAVA --> Right Atrium.
NECESSITY:
- The complete SEPARATION of oxygenated (left side) and deoxygenated (right side) blood ensures maximum oxygen delivery efficiency.
- This is essential for BIRDS and MAMMALS which are WARM-BLOODED and need high, constant energy to maintain body temperature.
- Without double circulation (as in amphibians/reptiles with 3-chambered hearts), oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, reducing oxygen delivery efficiency.

ANSWER:
XYLEM:
- MATERIAL TRANSPORTED: Water and dissolved minerals (inorganic salts).
- DIRECTION: One-way - UPWARD only (from roots to leaves and other parts).

- CELLS: Dead cells (vessels and tracheids) - no cytoplasm.
- ENERGY: Does NOT require metabolic energy (passive process).
- Flow: Continuous upward column of water.

PHLOEM:

- DIRECTION: BIDIRECTIONAL - both upward and downward (from leaves to all parts).

items.question: Compare the functioning of alveoli in the lungs and nephrons in the kidneys with respect to their structure and functioning.
items.answer:
ANSWER:
ALVEOLI (Lungs):
- STRUCTURE: Balloon-like air sacs; very thin walls (one cell layer); surrounded by capillaries; huge surface area (~80 m2).
- FUNCTION: GAS EXCHANGE - O2 from alveolar air diffuses into blood capillaries; CO2 from blood diffuses into alveoli to be exhaled.
- PROCESS: Diffusion (passive, no energy needed at exchange surface).
- FILTRATION: Separates useful gas (O2) from waste gas (CO2).
- END PRODUCT: Oxygenated blood; exhaled CO2.

NEPHRONS (Kidneys):
- STRUCTURE: Microscopic tubular units; Bowman's capsule (cup-shaped) + glomerulus (capillary tuft) + long renal tubule; surrounded by capillaries.
- FUNCTION: BLOOD FILTRATION - filters blood to remove nitrogenous wastes (urea); reabsorbs useful substances; produces urine.
- PROCESS: ULTRAFILTRATION (pressure-driven) + SELECTIVE REABSORPTION (active transport, requires ATP).
- FILTRATION: Separates waste (urea, excess salts) from useful substances (glucose, amino acids, most water).
- END PRODUCT: Urine (waste); cleansed blood.

SIMILARITIES:
- Both have thin walls for efficient exchange.
- Both are in contact with extensive capillary networks.
- Both are involved in maintaining the internal environment of the body (homeostasis).
- Both involve exchange of materials between blood and an external/internal environment.

DIFFERENCES:
- Alveoli: Gas exchange (passive diffusion). Nephrons: Liquid filtration (active + passive).
- Alveoli output: Gaseous CO2 exhaled. Nephrons output: Liquid urine.
- Alveoli do not require ATP for gas exchange. Nephrons require ATP for reabsorption.
